For a fast pass, Introduction + Section 3.1 + Figure 1 + the method overview + main ablations should be enough to capture the thesis in under an hour. For a serious assessment of whether this paradigm is worth following, the theory sections need a full read.41:T6ea,NESTOR introduces nested sparsity. The model first routes each token to a small subset of attention columns, and then, within each selected column, applies standard MoE-style expert routing in the feed-forward path. Concretely, each block contains C columns, and a column router selects Kc active columns per token. Each column has its own attention parameters and computes causal attention only over the subset of tokens routed into that column. This creates two kinds of attention-side sparsity at once: parameter sparsity, because a token only uses a subset of attention parameters, and map sparsity, because attention is computed only within the routed token subset. Inside each column, each layer then has E experts, of which Ke are selected by an expert router, giving the usual MoE sparsity on the MLP side. The effective computation path for a token is therefore hierarchical: column selection times expert selection. This differs from standard sparse-attention methods, which mainly reduce the attention map while keeping parameters shared, and from mixture-of-attention-head approaches, which often route attention more locally and independently per layer. NESTOR’s design is more structured: the attention subnetwork itself is conditionally selected, and that selection naturally nests with MoE routing. The paper emphasizes three distinct but coupled sparsity axes: attention-weight sparsity, attention-map sparsity, and expert sparsity. That framing is useful because it suggests the gains come not only from fewer FLOPs but from better allocation of model capacity. In continual pretraining, this structured routing may also help absorb new domains or longer contexts through specialized subpaths rather than by overwriting a large shared parameter core.42:T624,The experiments have two main parts. First is compute-efficient pretraining. The authors compare dense transformers, standard MoE transformers, and NESTOR across scales from roughly 100M to 1B active parameters. The headline result is that NESTOR achieves 1.13–1.29× better compute efficiency than MoE and 3.1–4.1× better than dense transformers, and the advantage does not appear to vanish as scale increases. The important signal here is the downward shift in the loss-vs-compute curve, not a single benchmark number. Second is continual pretraining. The models are adapted to several specialized domains, and the comparison tracks both gains on the new domains and retention on the original pretraining distribution. NESTOR reportedly gains about as much as MoE on each new domain while forgetting less, and it does so with fewer training FLOPs per token on the continual data. The long-context extension setup increases context length from 4k to as high as 64k, and NESTOR maintains its advantage over MoE when models receive equal amounts of continual-pretraining tokens. That control matters because long-context improvements are often confounded by extra adaptation compute. The abstract does not expose all absolute losses, downstream metrics, load-balancing numbers, or ablation details, but the full paper likely includes comparisons among partial variants that activate only one or two sparsity axes. Those ablations are central for judging whether the nested design is genuinely synergistic rather than just another sparse-attention plus MoE combination.43:T482,This one deserves more than a quick skim. Start with Figure 1 and the architecture section until the interaction between column routing and expert routing is fully clear; otherwise the rest can look like generic sparsity. Then read the scaling-law section carefully, focusing on whether the NESTOR-vs-MoE gap is stable across model sizes rather than on the best single point. After that, read the continual-pretraining and long-context-extension sections, paying attention to how forgetting is measured and how the authors control tokens and FLOPs in the adaptation stage. Finally, inspect the ablations: what happens when only attention-side sparsity is enabled, only expert sparsity is enabled, or both are combined; how sensitive the model is to the number of columns and active columns; and whether routing introduces instability, imbalance, or communication overhead. Expect 45–60 minutes for a solid first pass. The two deeper questions worth carrying forward are whether this routing pattern scales cleanly in distributed training, and how much of the gain comes from capacity allocation versus an inductive bias toward document-local structure.44:T733,The method has three main components. First, elastic expert dimensions. Each MoE expert is turned into a Matryoshka-style nested FFN: instead of training multiple independent experts at different widths, the same parameter tensors support several inner dimensions. During training, a target width D_k is sampled, and only the first D_k hidden channels are used in the expert’s SwiGLU computation. At inference, this allows deterministic slicing of the same checkpoint into smaller expert variants, reducing both parameter residency and activation cost. The paper also notes an important stability issue: shrinking the inner dimension changes the scale of the down-projected activations, which can disturb residual addition and RMSNorm statistics, so a compensation or rescaling mechanism is introduced. Second, adaptive sigmoid routing. Rather than top-k softmax routing, the router produces independent sigmoid gates for experts and compares them against a learned, task-conditioned threshold. This lets each token activate a variable number of experts. Harder tokens can use more experts, easier tokens fewer. Compared with top-k, this relaxes fixed-FLOP control but enables finer-grained compute allocation. Third, a dual-consistency objective. Because training sees multiple capacity views—different widths and different routing patterns—the model is regularized with an in-place self-distillation loss that aligns predictive distributions across these nested structures. The key point is that no external teacher and no post-training adaptation are required; the consistency signal is built into the original training run. In addition, the architecture includes a Direction-Aware Shared Expert computed in parallel, intended to capture translation-direction-specific shared patterns and reduce over-reliance on sparse experts alone.45:T54a,The experiments cover PhoMT for English–Vietnamese, WMT14 for English–German, multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain German–English benchmark. This gives the method a reasonable spread across bilingual, multilingual, and multi-domain heterogeneity. At a high level, the full-capacity EDWARD-NMT improves over Transformer Big and is competitive with recent lightweight MoE baselines. The more interesting result is on extracted subnetworks: the smallest variant, EDWARD-NMT-S, is not separately trained but sliced from the same checkpoint, yet still outperforms a dense Transformer Base. That is the main empirical support for the “train once, deploy anywhere” claim. The provided text does not include the full BLEU/COMET tables or parameter counts, but the critical ablations are easy to infer: removing elastic dimensions, reverting to top-k routing, and removing dual-consistency. The most informative results are likely not the absolute benchmark scores, but whether degradation under slicing is smooth, whether adaptive routing produces meaningful variation in active expert counts, and whether the consistency loss materially improves the smallest subnetworks. If the paper includes active-expert histograms, quality-versus-memory curves across width slices, and ablations on consistency regularization, those are the parts to focus on.46:T4ec,Cord is “confidence-anchored residual decoding.” Instead of replacing confidence decoding with a full token-level planner, it keeps the base confidence ranking (top-2 margin) and learns bounded geometric corrections:
- Residual families: (i) generation direction bias (left-to-right, right-to-left, etc.), (ii) proximity-to-revealed-context (local continuation vs non-local seeding), and (iii) two-sided infilling preference (positions bracketed by revealed context).
- A lightweight prompt-conditioned network outputs a low-dimensional coefficient matrix; state features of the partially revealed response modulate how residuals apply over time, enabling within-rollout phase changes (seed anchors early, fill locally later).
- Training avoids step-wise discrete actions. For each prompt, Cord samples a single coefficient matrix that deterministically induces the entire state-dependent reveal trajectory, then receives a sequence-level reward. This reframes learning as a contextual bandit in a low-dimensional continuous space, sidestepping temporal credit assignment and reducing variance.
- The dLLM backbone stays frozen; only ~0.53M policy parameters are trained. When coefficients are zero, Cord exactly reduces to the original confidence decoder.47:T777,The method has two coupled components: Multi-Router and Multi-View.

Multi-Router addresses expert ranking. Instead of one routing head, the model uses multiple independently initialized routing heads over the same shared expert pool. Each head produces sigmoid scores, and the post-sigmoid scores are summed before a single top-k selection. The post-sigmoid aggregation is important: if logits were summed before the nonlinearity, the result would collapse into a single linear scorer, losing the intended multi-view effect. No explicit diversity regularizer is added; different initializations are enough to break symmetry, and the routers develop differentiated preferences during training. Aggregation then allows an expert to be selected either because one router strongly favors it or because several routers moderately support it.

Multi-View goes one step further and uses those differentiated preferences to modulate expert computation. Summed scores alone discard the relative preference pattern across routers, even when the total score is the same. To preserve that information, each router is paired with a learned latent projection, forming one latent view per router. For each selected expert, the raw scores across routers are normalized to produce expert-specific mixing weights over these latent views. The mixed representation becomes that expert’s input before dispatch. Crucially, each selected expert still performs only one forward pass, so the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and communication volume remain unchanged.

The design sits between two extremes. Standard MoE is cheap but relies on a single routing perspective. Full or partial dense expert evaluation gives richer signals but increases compute. Multi-View tries to capture some of the benefit of richer expert assessment and conditionalized computation by reusing router preferences rather than evaluating more experts.48:T62e,The main training run uses a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens. The full Multi-View MoE improves the mean score over nine downstream tasks by 1.18 points over the baseline, reaching 34.25. The Multi-Router submodule alone gives a 0.6-point gain, which suggests that part of the improvement comes from better expert ranking and the rest from router-conditioned input construction.

The most informative evidence comes from routing diagnostics. The authors densely evaluate all experts and compare router score rankings against empirical expert-utility rankings. Multi-Router improves the global score-utility rank correlation by a relative 8.1%, and in the layer with the worst single-router alignment the relative gain is about 58%. That directly supports the paper’s premise that single-router ranking is often a poor proxy for actual expert usefulness.

The paper also includes a strong sanity check for the view-mixing mechanism. At the final MoE layer, if the mixing proportions are permuted across experts while keeping expert selection and output gates fixed, held-out NLL worsens by 0.01340 nats/token. Permuting the mixing proportions across tokens for the same expert also hurts NLL. This shows that the model is not ignoring the added mechanism; the correspondence between token, expert, and view mixture carries real predictive value.

Overall, the empirical story is coherent: Multi-Router improves selection quality, and Multi-View adds further gains by making expert computation depend on router-specific preferences without increasing the expert budget.49:T49d,Start with the introduction, especially the figure showing the mismatch between router scores and dense expert-utility rankings. That figure is the foundation of the whole paper. If the mismatch were weak, the rest of the method would be much less compelling.

Then read the method section with two questions in mind. First, why is post-sigmoid summation necessary, and why would summing logits fail to create genuinely different routing views? Second, how exactly is expert-specific input constructed before dispatch, and why does that not increase the number of expert forward passes? Those two details capture the main architectural idea.

In the experiments, prioritize three parts: the main 10B-A1B / 708B-token results, the routing score versus expert utility diagnostics, and the permutation tests for view mixing. The first tells you that the method helps, the second explains why, and the third shows that the added mechanism is functionally used by the trained model. For a quick pass, 30–45 minutes is enough. For a deeper evaluation of whether this belongs in a production MoE recipe, the appendix comparisons of alternative aggregation choices are worth reading too.4a:T633,The method, CLIK, is a context-conditioned parameter generator that emits LoRA weights for a frozen backbone. The design choice that stands out is joint generation. Instead of producing adapter fragments independently, CLIK first encodes the context with the frozen backbone itself and collects representations from all layers. A Transformer-based generator then uses cross-attention from adapter queries to these contextual representations and emits the full LoRA set jointly. The motivation is straightforward: LoRA updates live across multiple layers and modules, and long-context knowledge is unlikely to decompose cleanly into independent local pieces. Joint generation gives the model a way to coordinate updates across the network. At inference time, the generated LoRA is inserted into the frozen base model, and the model answers from a context-free query prompt. This makes the one-time cost of reading a document reusable across many later queries. The paper positions this especially for multi-turn settings, where repeated re-reading of long histories is costly. Another notable part is the analysis of generated adapters: the context-specific signal appears to concentrate in a compact substructure of the LoRA, suggesting that internalized knowledge may occupy a much smaller effective parameter subspace than the raw adapter size would imply. Relative to prior hypernetwork-style LoRA generation, the main differences are the focus on long contexts rather than short task descriptions, and the explicit modeling of cross-layer/module dependencies in one coherent adapter.4b:T4cf,The reported evaluation covers knowledge-grounded QA with both single-hop and multi-hop document settings, plus transfer to multi-turn dialogue without dialogue-specific training. The main empirical pattern is clear even from the available text: CLIK substantially outperforms the no-context base model and earlier hypernetwork-based generators, while still trailing a model that has full access to the original context at inference time. That is an important result because it frames CLIK as a new quality-cost tradeoff point rather than a full replacement for retrieval-style prompting. The paper also highlights two analysis results. First, the generated adapter transfers to multi-turn use, which suggests the method is not merely memorizing answer templates for one-shot QA. Second, intervention and distributional analyses indicate that the context-dependent component is concentrated in a compact LoRA substructure, which opens the door to more aggressive compression or partial-layer generation. A quick read is about 30 minutes; a serious read should include the analysis section, not just the headline results.4d:Ta87,核心做法是把 action grammar 编译成“可达前缀状态树”，并用一次 tree-causal 的并行前向把所有前缀状态的 next-action 分布一次性算出来。

1) 问题形式化：每轮在候选集合 A_x（k<=20，且用上下文验证的 single-token label 绑定）里选择 n=min(b,k) 个互异动作，输出被 grammar G_x 约束为一个 JSON array：forced syntax token 与“动作槽位”交替出现；槽位处还要 mask 掉已选动作以保证 distinct。传统 grammar-constrained decoding 需要对每个 emitted token 做一次依赖 forward，关键路径 D_serial = n + m_syn（文中 n=3 时约 9）。

2) 可达状态很浅：当 horizon n 有界时，串行 greedy 控制器在后续只会访问“前缀状态”（prefix states）。以 n=3 为例，一旦 a1 固定，后续只需要咨询 (a1) 以及 (a1,c) 这类前缀（c!=a1），总数是 O(k) 而不是指数。

3) 两步执行图：
- Root prefill：对 prompt + 开头 forced syntax 做一次前向，得到 slot-1 logits，并缓存 KV；用与串行相同的规则选出 a1。
- Tree-causal probe：把所有需要的前缀 continuation（每个 continuation 都是“串行解码在该前缀下会生成的 forced token 序列”，包括语法 token 与槽位位置）拼接成一个 batch-like 的长序列，在一次 forward 里计算。关键是构造 block-causal attention mask：每个“行”（一个前缀）只能 attend 到共享的 prompt KV 和它自己的祖先 token；同时使用与串行一致的 position ids，使得每个位置看到的 token ids / position ids / 可见祖先集合与串行完全一致。

4) Policy-exact 理论：
- Prefix-state lemma：若 tree-packed 与 serial 在某个前缀 ρ 上的 token ids、position ids、ancestor-visible attention set、参数一致，则每层 hidden state 一致，从而 logits 一致。
- Policy equivalence：在 matched mask/position/tie-breaking 下，tree probe 产生的每个前缀分布等于串行解码在该前缀下的分布；因此 greedy 链可以“算术恢复”（不需要生成 token）。作者也明确指出有限精度可能在 near-tie 时翻转选择（Sec 4.1）。

5) 额外能力：
- 由于 probe 暴露了多动作选择的 joint 偏好，作者把“无序集合选择”做成 order-marginalized 的 set posterior 推断，并用 branch-and-bound 给出 MAP set 的证书（避免常见的截断/启发式）。
- 用 AR-vs-unary 的 KL divergence 给出 unary shortcut（一次性打分 k 个 label、但失去对已选历史的条件化）带来的 expected-utility loss 上界（通过 Pinsker）。这提供了一个可操作的“何时可以用 unary”的判据。4e:T80f,The method compiles the controller’s constrained decoding process into two forward passes: one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe.

- Setup: At each round, candidates are bound to context-verified single-token labels (k<=20). The grammar forces a JSON array of exactly n=min(b,k) distinct labels, interleaving forced syntax tokens with label slots that mask already-used labels.

- Key observation: With bounded horizon n (deployment uses n=3), the serial greedy controller can only visit a small set of reachable prefix states. After fixing a1, the remaining consulted states are essentially (a1) and (a1,c) for c!=a1, i.e., O(k) states.

- Execution:
  1) Root prefill: run the prompt + opening forced syntax once, obtain slot-1 logits and KV cache, pick a1.
  2) Tree-causal probe: build all required prefix continuations (exactly the forced token sequences serial decoding would have produced for each prefix), concatenate them into one packed sequence, and run a single forward pass with a block-causal attention mask. Each row attends to the shared prompt KV and its own ancestors only, using serial position indices so that tokens/positions/visible ancestry match the serial run.

- Exactness argument:
  Prefix-state equivalence lemma: if token ids, position ids, ancestor-visible attention set, and parameters match for a prefix, hidden states (hence logits) match layer-by-layer.
  Policy equivalence theorem: with matched masks/positions/tie-breaking, the packed probe reproduces the serial controller’s logits at every reachable prefix state; the greedy chain is recovered arithmetically. The paper notes finite-precision can flip near ties.

- Extensions:
  * Order-marginalized set selection: since the probe exposes joint preferences, the paper performs exact unordered multi-action inference and certifies the MAP set via branch-and-bound.
  * Unary-vs-AR gap: computes KL(AR || unary) and uses Pinsker to bound expected-utility loss when using the “unary shortcut” (single prefill scoring all k labels but losing history dependence).4f:T833,实验重点围绕 acceptance length（AL）与 KV 预算的关系展开，因为 speculative decoding 的实际收益高度依赖 draft 被 target 接受的长度。论文主要在 SPEED-Bench 上评测，特别强调 32K 输入长度、带 reasoning 的长输出场景，这比很多只看短输出的压缩实验更贴近真实瓶颈。

最关键的结果是，在 4× KV 压缩、32K ISL 条件下，RIFT 能保留接近全缓存 draft 的 AL，而 SnapKV 掉得明显。具体数字：Qwen3.5-4B 作为 drafter、Qwen3.5-122B 作为 target 时，RIFT 最多保留 96% 的 full-cache AL；Nemotron3.5-Lightning 对 Nemotron3-Ultra 时保留 97%；而 SnapKV 在两组设置里只保留 63%–67%。这个差距已经不是小幅优化，而是说明静态 prefill 选择在长输出下确实会失效。

论文还展示了一个重要现象：随着 output sequence length 增长，SWA 会逐步追上并超过 SnapKV，说明“最近生成 token”的价值在长 decode 中持续上升，而 prefill 选出的 token 价值在衰减。作者把这作为 decode staleness 的直接证据。并且这种现象在 hybrid attention 模型里更明显，因为只有部分层保留 full attention 时，有限的全注意力层更依赖被保留下来的 KV 质量，错误选择的代价更高。

消融方面，值得注意的点有三个。第一，是否给预算显式分配 recency 槽位；没有这一步，重要性选择容易被 prompt token 占满。第二，refresh 频率与收益的关系；刷新越积极，AL 越高，但 latency 也上升，说明不存在单一最优点，而是部署相关的 Pareto 前沿。第三，compression-aware KD 的增益；它在相同压缩策略下进一步提高 draft-target 对齐，说明问题不只是检索哪些 KV，更是模型是否学会在受限上下文下工作。

从全文给出的设定看，作者也讨论了外部小 draft 与 KV-based self-speculation 两种场景，并说明 tail-augmented drafters 上压缩收益有限，因此没有把重点放在 MTP/Eagle 这类结构上。这一点让实验边界比较清楚。50:T414,Its value for foundation-model research is more than an inference-speed tweak. The paper turns a systems bottleneck into a modeling question: compressed context changes draft–target alignment, and that degradation has a clear temporal structure. That matters for long-context modeling, self-speculation, and any training setup where inference-time visibility is constrained. The contribution has three parts. First, it characterizes decode staleness and shows that prefill-only selection is not a robust solution once output length becomes large, especially in hybrid-attention models. Second, it proposes RIFT, which combines recency and importance instead of treating sliding-window and importance-based selection as mutually exclusive choices. Third, it adds compression-aware distillation so the drafter is trained under the same visibility constraints it will face at inference. This is not a paradigm shift, but within draft-side KV compression it is a fairly complete piece of work: diagnosis, method, and training fix are all present.51:T7df,The method has two components: RIFT at inference time, and compression-aware distillation during training.

On the inference side, the paper starts from two static extremes. One is pure sliding-window attention, which always keeps the most recent B tokens. The other is prefill-based selection, where a fixed subset of prompt KVs is chosen once using aggregated attention scores, as in SnapKV. Sliding window is strong on recency but weak on remote context. Prefill selection preserves long-range prompt information but becomes stale as decoding progresses. RIFT combines the two. The KV budget is explicitly split between recent generated tokens and importance-selected historical tokens. This preserves local continuity while still keeping a sparse set of long-range anchors.

The second idea is decode-time refresh. The importance-selected subset is not frozen after prefill; it can be recomputed periodically during generation. That lets the retained historical context adapt to the current decoding state. The trade-off is extra latency, so RIFT is presented as a family of strategies with different refresh frequencies and complexity/quality trade-offs.

The training-side contribution is compression-aware knowledge distillation. The authors argue that a drafter trained with full context but deployed with compressed context suffers from a substantial mismatch. To address this, they distill under compression-driven attention masks that mimic the inference-time cache restriction. The student is therefore optimized to match the teacher/target distribution under limited context visibility, rather than under an unrealistic full-cache condition.

Compared with prior work, SnapKV mainly relies on prefill importance and does not address relevance drift during decoding, while pure sliding window discards remote selection entirely. RIFT’s main difference is not a fancier scoring rule; it is the explicit treatment of time and the use of training to compensate for compression-induced distribution shift.52:T80b,The main metric is acceptance length (AL), which is the right quantity for speculative decoding because realized speedup depends heavily on how many draft tokens the target accepts. The evaluation focuses on SPEED-Bench, especially 32K input length with reasoning enabled, which makes output length long enough for KV bottlenecks and staleness effects to matter.

The headline result is that under 4× KV compression and 32K ISL, RIFT retains almost all of the full-cache drafter quality, while SnapKV drops sharply. With Qwen3.5-4B drafting for Qwen3.5-122B, RIFT retains up to 96% of full-cache AL. With Nemotron3.5-Lightning drafting for Nemotron3-Ultra, it retains 97%. SnapKV retains only 63%–67% in the same settings. That gap is large enough to support the paper’s central claim that static prefill-only selection breaks down in long-output decoding.

A key empirical pattern is that as output length increases, sliding-window attention catches up to and then surpasses SnapKV. This is direct evidence for decode staleness: the value of recent generated tokens keeps rising, while the value of a fixed prompt-based subset decays. The effect is stronger in hybrid-attention models, where the few full-attention layers become more sensitive to which KVs are retained.

The ablations highlight three useful points. First, explicitly reserving budget for recency matters; otherwise importance selection can be dominated by prompt tokens. Second, refresh frequency trades quality for latency, producing a deployment-dependent Pareto frontier rather than a single best operating point. Third, compression-aware KD gives additional gains on top of the same compression policy, showing that the problem is not only which KVs to keep, but whether the drafter has learned to operate under restricted context.

The paper also evaluates both external small drafters and KV-based self-speculation, and notes that tail-augmented drafters such as MTP/Eagle-like setups see limited benefit from this kind of compression, which helps define the scope of the method.53:T47a,For a quick read, focus on three parts.

First, read the introduction and the section on decode staleness. The most important figures are the ones showing AL as a function of output length. They make the central point clearly: prompt importance selected at prefill is not stable over long decoding trajectories.

Second, read the method section for the RIFT family. Pay attention to how the budget is split between recency and importance, when refresh is triggered, and how the variants differ in complexity. You do not need every implementation detail on a first pass; the main goal is to understand the design space.

Third, read the main results and ablations. Start with the 32K ISL, 4× compression tables, then the refresh and KD ablations. That is enough to separate gains from the compression policy itself versus gains from training compensation.

A 30–40 minute skim is enough to extract the main idea. If reading more deeply, the appendix sections on hybrid attention and on why tail-augmented drafters benefit little from KV compression are worth the extra time, because they define where the method is likely to matter in practice.54:T5b0,Key insight: selection outputs a discrete set of indices; top-k is non-differentiable, and backward only needs the k selected scores. Therefore, you can (i) avoid materializing the full score table and (ii) avoid rerunning selection during recomputation.

HyScale implements this via:
1) HyTopK: an on-the-fly, exact top-k operator that maintains top-k while scoring, eliminating the full score table. It is deterministic and CP-compatible. It uses a threshold-filtering idea with an “optimistic threshold” and a rare/cheap recovery path to keep exactness without slowing down.
2) Selection replay: record forward-pass selection results and, during activation recomputation, replay only the k selected entries needed for the indexer loss—rather than recomputing selection over all prior tokens. This moves recomputation granularity below the operator level to “only what the indexer loss needs.”
3) End-to-end integration on Megatron-LM: once selection is faster, CP communication and sparse kernels become visible bottlenecks. HyScale overlaps CP collectives for sparse attention behind selection (decoupled CP overlap) and introduces locality-aware sparse kernels that process adjacent queries together to reuse loads/updates for shared entries.

A notable design choice is insisting on exact top-k (vs sampling/approximation) for determinism and training stability, while using replay to avoid paying the recomputation cost of exact selection.55:T43f,Deep-read plan (1.5–2 hours):
1) Start with the Introduction and Figure 1 to internalize the two root causes: score-table materialization and recomputation repeating selection.
2) Read HyTopK carefully: how exact top-k is achieved in a streaming manner under CP; what “optimistic threshold + recovery” concretely means; how determinism is preserved.
3) Read selection replay in detail: what is stored from the forward pass (indices, selected scores, metadata), how recomputation reconstructs only what the indexer loss needs, and why this beats operator-level selective recomputation.
4) In the systems section, focus on (i) decoupled CP overlap scheduling/dep graph and (ii) locality-aware sparse kernel design (why adjacent-query processing reduces redundant memory traffic).
5) Validate generality via the DSA/CSA/QSA experiments: identify which assumptions are architecture-agnostic and which are specific to token-level sparsity.
If you only want the most reusable engineering idea: the replay interface and data structures around top-k indices are the highest-leverage parts.56:T41c,The main testbed is the MiniMax-H3 decoder: 2.4B parameters, 36 pre-norm ViT blocks, width 2048, SwiGLU MLPs, QK-RMSNorm, 3-axis RoPE, and four registers per tile. Its released tiling uses 16×16 latent-token tiles, corresponding to 256 pixels, with at least 64 pixels of overlap. At 704×1280 resolution, spatial overlap processes each token 2.03 times on average, so roughly half of per-token computation is duplicated. Larger tiles cause about an 11.9 dB drop, while reducing overlap to 16 pixels costs about 0.34 dB. Intervention results show that MiniMax-H3 needs 4 of 36 layers kept per tile, MAGI-1 needs 3 of 24, and ViTok-v2 needs none. TileShare-6 matches the released MiniMax-H3 decoder on PSNR, LPIPS, and DISTS on DAVIS while running 1.38–1.51× faster. On the held-out UVG confirmation set, TileShare-4 matches all three metrics, and TileShare-6 matches PSNR and DISTS while improving LPIPS. Short self-distillation can remove the remaining per-tile layers for MiniMax-H3.57:T8ee,方法核心是一个由 Taylor 一阶展开驱动的误差分解。作者把最终输出记为 O，把第 l 层注意力输出记为 A^(l)，把模型视为 O = G(A^(0), ..., A^(L-1))。当对某层 KV cache 做压缩时，会引入该层局部扰动 ΔA^(l)。在小扰动假设下，最终输出偏差可以用一阶多元 Taylor 展开近似，从而得到两类因素：

1）Local Approximation Error，记作 E_l：表示第 l 层压缩本身造成的信息损失。
2）Layer-wise Structural Sensitivity，记作 S_l：表示该层扰动经由后续网络被放大的程度，通常可由梯度范数或相关敏感度指标近似。

有了这个分解，系统设计就对应两条线。

第一条线是降低 E_l。作者认为现有 merging 方法的主要问题是忽略了 RoPE。RoPE 会对 query/key 施加位置相关旋转，导致 token 在旋转后的空间里不再适合直接按原始相似性做合并。于是他们把 token aggregation 放到 Pre-RoPE 的“安全区”，即在位置旋转之前进行聚合。为了避免简单合并导致注意力质量守恒被破坏，方法还引入 attention-conserving logit bias，在物理合并 token 时尽量保持原有注意力质量分布。这里的直觉是：不是只保留 token 数量，而是尽量保留被这些 token 支撑的注意力质量。

第二条线是管理 S_l。作者不满足于知道哪些层敏感，而是把 memory management 写成动态资源调度问题：在总内存固定、希望达到近似 O(1) 占用的前提下，按层分配不同 KV budget。具体做法是利用 offline gradient priors 估计各层敏感度，然后把更多预算留给高敏感层，从低敏感层更激进地回收内存。这样做的含义是，压缩不再是所有层一刀切，而是层感知的非均匀分配。

整体上，这是一个 hybrid framework：Pre-RoPE aggregation 负责减少局部误差，sensitivity-aware budget allocation 负责抑制误差放大。它是 training-free、model-agnostic 的，不需要重新训练底座模型。和已有方法相比，区别主要有三点：一是给了一个明确的误差分析，而不是纯经验规则；二是把合并位置前移到 RoPE 前；三是预算分配按层敏感度动态调度，而不是固定比例压缩。58:T8f8,The method starts from a first-order Taylor analysis. Let the final model output be O and the attention output at layer l be A^(l). The model is abstracted as O = G(A^(0), ..., A^(L-1)). Compressing the KV cache at layer l introduces a local perturbation ΔA^(l). Under a small-perturbation assumption, the final output deviation can be approximated by a first-order multivariate Taylor expansion, yielding two factors:

1) Local Approximation Error E_l: the information loss caused directly by compression at layer l.
2) Layer-wise Structural Sensitivity S_l: how strongly perturbations at layer l are amplified by the rest of the network, estimated through gradient-based signals or related sensitivity measures.

This decomposition drives two design components.

The first component minimizes E_l. The authors argue that many existing merging methods ignore the effect of RoPE. Since RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys, the post-RoPE space is no longer a clean space for similarity-based token merging. Their solution is to perform token aggregation in a Pre-RoPE 'safe zone,' before positional rotation. To avoid losing attention mass during physical token consolidation, they introduce an attention-conserving logit bias so that the merged representation better preserves the original attention distribution.

The second component manages S_l. Instead of using a uniform compression ratio across layers, the paper formulates memory management as a dynamic resource scheduling problem under a fixed memory budget. Offline gradient priors are used to estimate layer sensitivity, and more KV budget is assigned to high-sensitivity layers while low-sensitivity layers are compressed more aggressively. In other words, compression becomes layer-aware rather than uniform.

Overall, the framework is hybrid: Pre-RoPE aggregation reduces local approximation error, and sensitivity-aware budget allocation controls downstream error amplification. It is training-free and model-agnostic, so it does not require retraining the base model. Compared with prior work, the differences are clear: an explicit error decomposition instead of pure heuristics, merging before RoPE rather than after it, and non-uniform layer-wise budget scheduling instead of fixed-ratio compression.59:T5e1,The headline result is explicit in the paper: on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Video-MemComp improves overall accuracy from 62.3% to 64.1% while limiting the average KV cache to 6,000 tokens per layer, reducing KV-cache memory by more than 90%. This is the paper’s 'less is more' result: removing redundant or harmful history can improve accuracy rather than merely preserving it.

The evaluation is conducted on benchmarks including MLVU, Video-MME, and EgoSchema, and across multiple MLLM architectures. The experiments support four main claims. First, under very low memory budgets, the method can match or even surpass the full-cache baseline. Second, the gains come from both parts of the design: Pre-RoPE aggregation lowers local approximation error, while layer-wise budget allocation reduces error accumulation. Third, layer sensitivity is highly non-uniform, so uniform compression across layers is suboptimal. Fourth, RoPE-aware handling matters; merging after RoPE performs worse.

The most informative ablations are likely the following: with and without Taylor-guided sensitivity, with and without the Pre-RoPE safe zone, with and without the attention-conserving logit bias, fixed versus dynamic budget allocation, and accuracy-memory curves under different cache budgets. Even without reproducing every table entry, the main message is clear: the method does not rely on extra training to recover performance; it improves memory efficiency by making compression itself more principled at inference time.5a:T654,Read this paper by first understanding the analytical motivation, then the engineering choices.

Start with the introduction and the beginning of the method section. The first-order Taylor expansion is not there as a formal theorem; it is there to produce an actionable surrogate objective that separates local compression loss from layer sensitivity. Once that framing is clear, the rest of the method becomes easy to follow.

Then read the Pre-RoPE aggregation section carefully. Two questions matter: why the post-RoPE space is a poor place for token merging, and how the attention-conserving logit bias compensates for changes in attention mass after merging. This is the most distinctive engineering idea in the paper.

After that, read the layer-wise budget allocation section. The key issue is not the optimizer details, but how offline gradient priors are estimated, how budgets are assigned, whether calibration data is needed, and whether sensitivity is stable across samples. This part is highly transferable to long-context text LMs.

In the experiments, prioritize the main table, the memory-accuracy tradeoff curves, and the ablation tables. If the goal is only to decide whether the paper is worth following up, 25-35 minutes is enough. If the goal is to adapt the idea to text LMs or unified multimodal LMs, spend another 20 minutes on the appendix for implementation details, complexity analysis, and sensitivity visualizations. The most interesting open question is whether the sensitivity prior can be updated online, or even reflected in pretraining so that representations become easier to compress.5b:T448,The paper asks a narrow but important question: do halting heads in looped language models actually convert low predicted iteration counts into real compute savings at inference time? The answer is often no. The mismatch comes from two places. First, the standard training objective is misaligned with the execution rule. With the common mixture loss, the halting head is trained through a mixture of hidden states from all iterations, while inference stops on one discrete iteration chosen by a thresholded cumulative halting rule. So the model can report low expected halting steps yet still run almost to the cap under the actual stopping rule. Second, batching changes the compute story again: even if some tokens halt early, the batch waits for the deepest token, so average token depth is not the same as realized batched compute. The paper is therefore not just about adaptive depth in the abstract. It is about where the training objective, stopping rule, and execution system fail to line up, how large that gap is, and how halting should be evaluated if one wants honest compute claims.5c:T40a,This matters for pretraining-oriented model design because looped LMs and recurrent-depth LMs are often motivated by the promise of adaptive compute without extra parameters. The paper shows that this promise can be overstated if one reports only expected halting steps. More broadly, it is a clean case study of train-test mismatch in adaptive computation: a probabilistic training signal does not automatically translate into useful discrete decisions at inference. That lesson extends beyond looped LMs to early-exit transformers, pondering methods, and other conditional-compute schemes. It also contributes a practical reporting standard: expected steps, realized steps under a stated exit rule, and batched execution depth should all be reported. Finally, the paper proposes a pre-head diagnostic that estimates how much a halting mechanism could help before one spends effort training it. The contribution is not a new architecture. It is a careful correction to how this line of work should be trained, compared, and measured.5d:T7c9,The technical contribution is mainly analytical and experimental. First, the authors dissect the standard ACT-style mixture loss. In that setup, the language-model loss is computed from a hidden state formed by mixing representations from all iterations according to halting probabilities. This is convenient for optimization, but it gives the model access to a representation that is never available at inference, where the token exits at one concrete iteration. The paper quantifies this mismatch by replacing the mixture readout with the actual single-step state and showing a substantial degradation. Second, the authors test a PonderNet-style per-step loss, where every iteration is scored and the losses are weighted by the head’s own halting probabilities. This is much closer to the real execution path because the model is trained on all possible exit points. But the paper shows that this alone is still insufficient. Without a strong prior favoring early stopping, the learned distribution remains too conservative and realized savings stay weak. Section 6.2 is especially useful: the issue is not simply whether one supervises every step, but that the head also controls the weighting over steps, which encourages a self-consistent allocation of probability mass toward later iterations. Third, the evaluation protocol is upgraded from token-level expectations to actual execution. The paper separately measures expected halting steps, realized steps under the thresholded exit rule, and the number of iterations a batched pass really executes. This separation is central because it isolates three different objects that are often conflated. The paper also discusses a deployment detail that turns out to matter: in single-sequence generation, halted tokens have no fresh KV states for skipped iterations, yet later tokens may still attend to them there. Reusing halted tokens’ KV states is therefore treated as part of the method definition, not a minor implementation choice.5e:T8cb,The study trains looped models from 140M to 1.3B parameters, on two text corpora, mostly with three seeds, using a cap of 8 iterations. The main findings are consistent and fairly sharp. (1) With mixture-loss training, heads often predict fewer than 4 out of 8 iterations on average, but under the standard 90% cumulative-probability exit rule the realized depth remains close to the full 8. In other words, the headline expected depth reduction does not translate into actual compute reduction. (2) Forcing earlier stopping hurts quality quickly. Once the saving exceeds roughly one iteration, a same-size sampled-depth baseline—trained without a halting head, simply with randomly chosen iteration counts—outperforms the halting model at the same compute budget. That is a strong baseline result because it shows the halting mechanism can lose to a simpler training recipe on the quality-compute frontier. (3) The train-test mismatch is large in language-model terms: replacing the mixture state with the actual single-step state costs about 0.2 BPB, while the gap between the smallest and largest models in the paper is about 0.24 BPB. So the mismatch is not a minor artifact; it is comparable to a substantial scaling gain. (4) Per-step loss only works when paired with a strong early-stop prior. Without that prior, the objective is more faithful to inference but still does not produce useful realized savings. (5) Batching removes most of the remaining advantage. On whole-text evaluation, the per-step model can beat the sampled-depth baseline at matched average depth; in generation with batches of 32 sequences, the actual batch depth rises well above the average token depth and most of the advantage disappears. (6) The same phenomenon is observed for Ouro, a released looped LM with a trained halting head. (7) In single-sequence generation, some benefit survives if halted tokens’ KV states are reused across skipped iterations, but even then the model does not beat a specialist trained to run at a fixed depth of about three iterations. The experimental arc is well structured: invalidate the common metric, identify the loss-level cause, add the systems-level effect, and compare against simpler baselines under matched compute.5f:T427,For a quick but useful read, start with the Introduction and Figures 1–2. The authors use OpenCode as a fixed agent scaffold and implement five compaction strategies as drop-in replacements for the default compaction logic. They then evaluate four frontier models on three realistic long-horizon benchmarks. The study is organized around four questions. First, threshold sensitivity: they sweep the token threshold that triggers compaction, from 160K to 380K, and measure downstream task performance. Second, strategy sensitivity: they compare default self-summarization against alternatives such as using a smaller model to summarize, removing reasoning blocks, and writing the pre-compaction context to disk as a near-lossless external memory. Third, constraint retention: on tasks with explicit anti-cheating rules, they inspect how many constraints survive the first and subsequent compactions. Fourth, benchmark bias: they compare benchmark trajectories with real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat to see which kinds of information are disproportionately lost. The contribution is less about a new algorithm and more about turning compaction from an implementation detail into a measurable experimental factor.61:T64d,The evaluation covers PaperBench, ProgramBench, and PostTrainBench, using Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, with two runs per task/configuration. Several results stand out. First, for the 1M-context models, changing the compaction threshold from 160K to 380K does not materially affect task performance. GPT-5.3-Codex, with a smaller 400K context window, degrades more clearly at lower thresholds on PaperBench and shows a weaker similar trend on PostTrainBench. Second, no compaction strategy consistently beats default self-summarization, including the near-lossless strategy that writes the full pre-compaction context to disk. This suggests that preserving information externally is not enough; the model must also know when and how to retrieve and reconstruct state from it. Third, more aggressive strategies can hurt some models substantially: removing reasoning blocks or summarizing with a smaller model can cost up to about 20 points on PaperBench for certain models, while leaving others nearly unchanged. That model-specific interaction is one of the most useful findings. Fourth, on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops roughly one of the task’s three anti-cheating rules on average, and the loss compounds with repeated compactions. Fifth, in real SWE-chat sessions, compaction drops instructions about how the agent should work, and what it should avoid doing, about six times more often than it drops specifications of what to build. That result explains why benchmark outcomes can look reassuring while real interactive use remains fragile.62:T43c,GS-MoE compresses experts along two axes. The first axis is groupwise subspace sharing. Experts are partitioned into groups, and each group has its own shared projection matrices. Each expert keeps expert-specific projections inside the group subspace, so the method does not force every expert in a layer to use one common basis. The second axis is intermediate-width compression. Each expert keeps a different number of hidden neurons, selected using ridge-leverage scores. The up projections are fit through a group-level surrogate and expert input statistics. For the down projections, the reconstruction objective has a closed-form solution before width compression, and Nyström reconstruction maps retained hidden activations into the shared coordinates. Capacity allocation is also calibration-driven: per-expert reconstruction-error reductions guide grouping, while a gradient-free layer-importance score based on normalized, gate-weighted expert output magnitudes guides budget allocation across layers. Eigenvalue-based scores and parameter costs further guide group ranks.63:T51b,BiLoCo approximates each weight matrix as W ≈ R + \sum_{i=1}^{r} \alpha_i (v_i u_i^T), where R is the NVFP4-quantized residual and u_i, v_i are binary sign vectors in {±1} (bit-packed), plus per-component scalar coefficients \alpha_i. Inference then replaces multiply-accumulate in the correction with sign-controlled add/subtract accumulations, which maps naturally to CUDA cores.

A key algorithmic issue is that the optimal sign-vector decomposition is not given by SVD. The paper fits rank-one components greedily (following prior sign-decomposition work): initialize signs randomly, alternate updates of u and v for a few steps, compute the best scale \alpha for that component, subtract it from the residual, and repeat. After all components are fitted, it re-solves all \alpha jointly via least squares to account for overlap/correlation among components, then quantizes the remaining residual to NVFP4.

On the systems side, the implementation is a fused single kernel on Blackwell: the main NVFP4 GEMM runs on Tensor Cores; the binary correction is computed on CUDA cores within the same launch; the correction is added in the GEMM epilogue. The design is explicitly motivated by decode-shape behavior where Tensor Cores are memory-stalled and CUDA cores can be overlapped rather than contended.64:T4ca,NgramRL uses the policy’s own recent rollouts as a free, self-updating drafter.
- Empirical observation: GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps/epochs and the policy changes incrementally, so completions for a given prompt are highly repetitive over time. The paper quantifies this locality (48–96% coverage of a later rollout by a prior one; recurring spans of 7–23 tokens).
- Drafter: a per-prompt n-gram table built from a bounded window of recent rollouts. Given the current context, it proposes continuations via lookup (model-free), and the target policy verifies them using standard speculative decoding accept/reject, preserving the exact output distribution.
- Runtime co-design: naive CPU-host lookup can serialize with GPU decoding, causing large GPU idle due to host round trips. NgramRL introduces an asynchronous multipath prefetcher: during GPU verification, the CPU prefetches drafts for likely next-step verification outcomes (indexed by outcome states such as (j, b)). An adaptive fan-out policy (a causal budget allocator) decides which branches to prefetch so most steps avoid post-verification host synchronization; uncovered branches fall back to synchronous lookup without changing semantics.65:T502,Two components.
1) LEMS (Layer-wise Error Modeling Search): instead of allocating ranks using uncalibrated local sensitivity metrics, LEMS builds a layerwise surrogate that mixes (a) local sensitivity/importance, (b) global layer importance, and (c) an explicit bias term to account for error accumulation/propagation through depth. With this surrogate, the rank allocation under a global parameter/rank budget is formulated as an ILP, enabling principled global search rather than greedy allocation.
2) KFAC-SVD: starts from Fisher-weighted SVD where the loss increase is approximated by a second-order expansion with the Hessian approximated by the Fisher matrix, then uses a Kronecker-factored approximation F ≈ A ⊗ G to obtain a Frobenius objective in whitened coordinates (G^{1/2} W A^{1/2}). The key change is how A and G are estimated: token-wise statistics rather than sequence-wise aggregation. The motivation is that sequence-level aggregation yields low effective rank under limited samples (rank collapse), while token-wise accumulation increases statistical support and stabilizes the Kronecker factors, improving the truncated SVD fidelity. The final compressed layer is implemented as two consecutive dense linear layers (C(Bx)), keeping inference kernels simple.66:T87c,方法名是 TraceQuery。整体结构可以概括成“trajectory-guided sparse decoding”。论文先做了一个因果链分析：representation error 会先扰动 decoding decision，再导致 trajectory divergence，最后才体现为质量下降。因此如果预算有限，直接围绕 future decisions 分配 fresh computation，比单纯压低表示误差更有效。

具体做法分两部分。

第一部分是监督信号构造。作者对同一个样本运行 full-denoising decoding，得到一个无 cache 近似误差的参考轨迹。这个轨迹给出了每个 unresolved position 在未来何时会被提交，或者说它离“即将成为关键决策点”有多近。TraceQuery 不试图搜索最优轨迹，也不强行让推理时完全跟随 reference trajectory，而是把这个 full-denoising trajectory 当作 router 的训练标签：学习在当前解码状态下，对 unresolved positions 做 near-future relevance ranking。

第二部分是推理时的稀疏查询。在线推理时，模型不会对所有 unresolved positions fresh recompute，而是先从当前可廉价获得的 decoding-state signals 中提取特征，由一个轻量 router 预测哪些位置最值得查询。被选中的少量 candidates 才会重新计算表示；其余位置继续复用 cache。随后 backbone dLLM 只在这些 freshly evaluated candidates 中决定最终 commit 哪个位置或哪些位置。这里有一个很重要的拆分：router 只负责“算哪里”，backbone 仍负责“提交什么”。这样做比直接让 router 决定 commit 更稳，因为最终决策仍由原模型完成，避免轻量模块过度接管生成。

从论文表述看，这个框架适用于 single-block 和 block-wise diffusion decoding。它也兼容现有 cache-based sparse decoding setting，但目标函数变了：不是最小化 cache reuse induced representation error，而是最大化对 full-denoising near-future trajectory 的覆盖。作者强调使用的是当前状态下可便宜获得的信号，因此 router 本身的额外开销应当较小，重点是用少量 fresh token computations 换更接近 full denoising 的轨迹。67:T40f,The main value is conceptual as much as practical. For diffusion LM inference, it shifts the optimization target from “repairing cached states” to “spending compute on positions that matter for the upcoming decoding trajectory.” That is a better fit for iterative non-AR generation, where small early decision errors can compound over many denoising steps. A second contribution is methodological: the full-denoising run is turned into a supervision source for query allocation. Instead of treating full denoising only as an expensive reference, the method learns from it which unresolved positions are near-future critical. This is useful beyond the specific implementation here. Any iterative LM that alternates approximate state reuse with selective recomputation could potentially benefit from a trajectory-aware control policy. In terms of contribution type, this is not a new pretraining paradigm, but it is a meaningful inference-side improvement for diffusion LM systems, especially where quality-compute trade-offs matter.68:T869,The method, TraceQuery, is framed as trajectory-guided sparse decoding. The paper first proposes a causal view of cached decoding errors: representation error perturbs decoding decisions; perturbed decisions cause trajectory divergence; trajectory divergence then leads to quality loss. Under a limited compute budget, directly targeting the decision layer is therefore more efficient than uniformly reducing representation error.

The method has two key components.

First, it constructs supervision from full-denoising trajectories. For a given example, the model is run in full-denoising mode, producing a reference trajectory without cache-induced approximation. This trajectory tells us which unresolved positions are likely to become important soon—effectively a notion of near-future relevance. TraceQuery does not try to search for an optimal trajectory, nor does it force inference to exactly follow the reference. Instead, it trains a lightweight router to rank unresolved positions according to how soon they matter along the full-denoising path.

Second, at inference time, the router uses inexpensive signals available from the current decoding state to select a small fresh-query set. Only those candidate positions are recomputed from scratch; all other unresolved positions continue to reuse cached representations. The backbone dLLM then makes the actual commit decision among the freshly evaluated candidates. This separation is important: the router decides where to spend computation, while the backbone retains control over what to commit. That design keeps the lightweight module from directly taking over semantic generation decisions.

The framework is described as applicable to both single-block and block-wise diffusion decoding. It is compatible with the general cache-based sparse decoding setup, but changes the objective. Instead of minimizing cache-induced representation error, it tries to maximize alignment with the near-future full-denoising trajectory. The practical premise is that the router can operate on cheap state features, so the extra overhead remains small relative to the saved fresh token computations.69:T6ca,The experimental story is centered on quality-compute trade-offs and trajectory analysis rather than on a single scalar metric. Several conclusions are clearly stated in the provided full text.

1. Trajectory deviation explains quality loss better than representation error alone. The paper shows that cached decoding can still deviate from the full-denoising unmask order even when token-level predictions largely agree. This means local agreement is not enough; the decoding path itself matters.

2. Recovering longer prefixes of the full-denoising trajectory improves quality. This is an important intervention result: the more the decoding process is anchored to the reference trajectory, the better the output quality. It suggests strong path dependence, especially from early commitments.

3. A single learned router generalizes across tasks, model variants, and diffusion LM families, approaching full-denoising quality while using substantially fewer fresh token computations. This is the main empirical claim and is stronger than a narrow single-model result.

4. Compared with cache-based baselines using fixed or heuristic refresh policies, TraceQuery improves the quality-computation frontier: better quality at similar compute, or lower recomputation at similar quality.

When reading the full paper, the most important details to verify are the router features, the query budget definition, the shape of the quality-vs-compute curves, the gap to heuristic baselines, and whether cross-family generalization requires retraining the router.6a:T5c5,This is a skim-level paper, but the motivation section deserves careful attention. Start with the introduction and the trajectory analysis around Figure 1. That is where the paper earns its premise. If you skip that part, TraceQuery may look like just another learned cache policy. The actual distinction is that it optimizes trajectory adherence rather than representation fidelity.

Then read the method overview and Figure 2. The key design choice is the split between the router and the backbone: the router allocates fresh computation; the backbone still makes the final commit decision. That separation is likely a major reason the method remains stable.

Next, inspect how the supervision labels are derived from full-denoising trajectories and what cheap decoding-state features are fed into the router. In the experiments, focus on three groups of figures: quality vs fresh-computation curves, trajectory deviation analyses, and ablations on query budget, feature design, reference-prefix recovery, and single-block vs block-wise settings. If the goal is only to understand the idea, 30–45 minutes should be enough. If the goal is to assess adoption in a real dLLM stack, the appendix details on router training and runtime overhead are necessary.6b:T724,The setup is formalized as follows. Let q be the parallel drafter with block length L. Its distribution at position l, q_l(.|c), depends only on the current context c. The verifier p is autoregressive, so its distribution at the same position is p_l(.|c, x_<l), which depends on the sampled prefix inside the current draft block. Therefore, for a fixed student head q_l, different sampled drafts induce different teacher distributions. Existing on-policy distillation methods effectively supervise the same student prediction with these separate, potentially conflicting conditional targets. This creates an averaging problem: the student is asked to imitate multiple incompatible teacher views while lacking access to the within-block prefix that generated them.

MDraft solves this by aggregating verifier feedback across multiple drafts before constructing the training target. Intuitively, it tries to estimate which tokens are broadly useful for acceptance at a given position under the distribution of plausible prefixes, rather than which token is preferred under one particular sampled prefix. That is a better match to the structure of the parallel drafter, because the drafter cannot observe those prefixes in the first place.

The key contribution is therefore not a new model architecture but a new teacher-target construction for on-policy distillation. Instead of forcing an autoregressive conditional distribution directly onto a prefix-agnostic parallel student, MDraft approximates a marginal target over multiple sampled drafts. The paper’s argument is strong on this point: if the real objective is to maximize speculative acceptance rather than to minimize teacher cross-entropy under a mismatched conditioning structure, then the training target should reflect acceptance utility across possible prefixes.6c:T4a5,The main metric is acceptance length, not standard language-model perplexity. The authors fine-tune parallel drafters and evaluate them on mathematical, coding, and conversational benchmarks. MDraft achieves the best overall mean acceptance length among the on-policy distillation baselines considered, meaning that the verifier accepts more drafted tokens per pass and speculative decoding becomes more efficient. The abstract does not expose the full numeric table, but the body indicates that the gains are consistent across task types rather than confined to a single domain.

More importantly, the experiments support the mechanism claim. When verifier targets from different sampled prefixes are distilled separately, the student becomes overly conservative and acceptance drops. Aggregating verifier information across multiple drafts produces a student distribution that better matches what the verifier is willing to accept in actual use. If you read the full paper, the most informative ablations are likely the number of drafts used for aggregation, the block length L, and the exact aggregation rule, since these directly test whether the method is solving the stated mismatch.6d:T85e,方法由三个部件组成。第一，候选块构造。给定当前前缀 p，先用浅层或当前可读出的预测得到一个 head token h，然后在 p∥h 中做 suffix matching，寻找此前上下文里与末尾后缀最长匹配的位置；从该位置向后复制最多 K 个 token 作为 tail，形成候选块 B=(b0,...,bk)，其中 b0=h。若找不到匹配，就退化成单 token 块。这里借鉴了 prompt lookup decoding 的思路，但不是直接把复制结果当最终输出，而是把它当 speculative proposal。

第二，浅层筛查。候选块整体先推进到 screening depth ds，而不是直接跑满总深度 D。在 ds 处，用每个前驱位置的 shallow next-token prediction 去检查后继 copied token 是否一致。具体是找从 head 开始的最长连续通过前驱预测校验的前缀；通过的部分保留，后缀立即裁掉，并释放其 KV / hidden state。这个设计比最终深度才发现错误更省，因为错误复制通常会在较早位置暴露，没必要让整段错误 tail 继续消耗深层 recurrent 计算。

第三，连续调度与因果提交。保留下来的 token 继续向更深层推进，同时最近一个保留位置立刻作为下一块的起点，允许新块在旧块尚未 full-depth 验证完成时进入流水线。最终只有达到 full depth 的位置才按因果顺序提交输出。论文强调，真正的收益来自 shallow screening 和 continuous scheduling 的配合：如果只是筛查但不让新块提前进入，流水线填充不足；如果只连续推进但不筛查，错误复制会污染后续深层计算，浪费算力。

与已有 self-speculative decoding 的区别主要有三点。其一，draft 来源不同：不是中间层逐 token 生成，而是“一个新 head + 一段上下文复制 tail”的块级 proposal。其二，验证粒度不同：不是只在 full depth 做接受/拒绝，而是在浅层先做 predecessor-consistency screening。其三，调度方式更偏向 recurrent pipeline，而不是传统 draft-then-verify 两阶段流程。整个方法 training-free，直接复用现有 readout。6e:T8ee,The method has three main components. First, block construction. Given a prefix p, the model predicts a fresh head token h. Then CopyLoop performs suffix matching over p concatenated with h, looking for the longest matching suffix in earlier context, similar in spirit to prompt lookup decoding. From the matched location it copies up to K following tokens as a tail, producing a candidate block B=(b0,...,bk) with b0=h. If no useful match exists, it falls back to a single-token block.

Second, shallow screening. Instead of sending the whole candidate block directly through the full recurrent depth D, the block is advanced only to a screening depth ds<D. At that depth, each copied token is checked against the shallow next-token prediction of its immediate predecessor. The algorithm keeps the longest prefix of copied tokens that agrees with predecessor predictions and prunes the remaining suffix immediately, including its KV and hidden-state footprint. This is the key efficiency move: copied tails are cheap to propose, but many are partially wrong, so the method tries to detect disagreement before deep recurrent compute is spent.

Third, continuous scheduling with causal commitment. Tokens that survive screening continue toward full-depth verification, while the latest retained position immediately seeds the next candidate block. This allows newer blocks to enter the pipeline before earlier ones finish full verification. Final outputs are still committed only in causal order once they reach full depth. The paper argues that the gain comes from the interaction between shallow screening and continuous scheduling: screening alone saves some wasted deep compute, but scheduling is what turns that into latency reduction; scheduling alone would let many bad copied tails consume deeper passes.

Compared with prior self-speculative decoding, the differences are clear. Drafts are not generated token by token from intermediate passes; they are block proposals composed of one fresh head plus a copied tail. Verification is not only a final accept/reject step; there is an explicit shallow recurrent filter. And the execution pattern is a recurrent pipeline rather than a clean two-stage draft/verify setup. The method is training-free and uses existing model readouts.6f:T577,The evaluation covers six checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn looped-Transformer families: four Base models and two Thinking models, on code generation and mathematical reasoning workloads. Relative to full-depth autoregressive decoding, CopyLoop reports 2.98-10.70x speedups on Base models and 2.74-3.52x on Thinking models. It outperforms all baselines in 14 of 16 Base model-task settings and in all 8 Thinking settings, while keeping task accuracy close to standard decoding.

The ablations are more informative than the headline numbers. The paper shows that shallow screening becomes much more valuable when paired with continuous scheduling, which supports the claim that the algorithm is not just prompt lookup plus verification. Hyperparameter studies suggest that screening depth ds, copy length K, and suffix-match settings transfer with only light calibration across model families.

The analysis section also clarifies where the method works best. Speedups increase with longer generations and with more reusable spans in context, because copied tails are more likely to be valid and the pipeline has time to amortize setup overhead. Short responses benefit less. Thinking models see smaller gains than Base models, which is plausible: reasoning-heavy outputs are less repetitive and intermediate predictions are less stable, so copied proposals are harder to validate cheaply.70:T407,Start with the introduction and Figure 1. That equation captures the acceptance rule and explains why shallow verification is cheap.

If the goal is to decide whether to reproduce it on an in-house recurrent model, Figure 1, the algorithm description, the main results table, and the key ablations are enough.71:T72a,The core method is Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), an extension of the earlier R-SWA design. In Unlimited OCR, text history was already constrained to a fixed sliding window, so text-side memory no longer grew with document length. The remaining problem was the visual side: the decoder still attended to all page tokens globally. SR-SWA makes that visual reference path sparse and bounded.

The mechanism is hierarchical. First comes Page Gate. Instead of exposing every page to every query, the model selects relevant pages at the page level. This is not just top-k retrieval in a naive sense; it must preserve multi-page positional relationships and cross-page structural continuity, otherwise page-spanning tables, paragraph continuations, headers, and similar structures would break. Second comes Token Sieve. Even within the selected remote pages, the model does not attend to all tokens. It groups tokens into buckets and keeps only the top-k remote buckets for attention. The design matches the empirical structure of long documents: dependencies are sparse across pages and concentrated within local regions.

At the system level, SR-SWA is combined with the Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm so that per-step decoding latency remains bounded as the number of pages grows. The backbone inherits the Unlimited OCR / DeepSeek OCR stack: a DeepEncoder plus an MoE decoder with 3B total parameters and about 500M activated parameters per token. An important point is that the speedup does not come from shrinking the model. It comes from changing the attention access pattern from “attend to all visual tokens” to “route at the page level, then filter at the token-bucket level.” That is more principled than simple truncation because it still preserves long-range cross-page references when needed.72:T631,The experiments have two main threads. The first is efficiency. The paper claims near-constant per-step decoding latency even in the hundred-page regime, which is the primary objective of SR-SWA. The second is accuracy. In addition to existing multi-page benchmarks, the authors introduce MarathonDocBench, a new benchmark for hundred-page document parsing. It contains 100 documents spanning 103 to 300 pages with about 205k annotated layout elements. This matters because the benchmark pushes evaluation from “can it handle tens of pages” to “can it preserve structure and content over hundreds of pages.”

From the provided full-text excerpt, Unlimited OCR 2 outperforms the previous Unlimited OCR setup and other end-to-end baselines on long-horizon parsing while avoiding the usual accuracy collapse that can come with aggressive sparsification. The paper also emphasizes that MarathonDocBench contains much denser cross-page text and table continuations than earlier benchmarks, making it a stronger test of whether page-level sparsity misses long-range dependencies.

The excerpt does not include the full result tables, so exact latency numbers, throughput values, and benchmark-by-benchmark score deltas cannot be quoted reliably here. The hard details that are visible are: the backbone uses a 3B MoE decoder with 500M activated parameters per token, and MarathonDocBench contains 100 documents, 103–300 pages each, with 205k annotated elements. The main empirical claim is length-invariant per-step latency together with stable accuracy in the hundred-page regime.73:T4b0,For a quick read, start with the introduction and lock in the problem framing: Unlimited OCR solved growing text history, but not growing visual history; Unlimited OCR 2 makes the visual side bounded as well. Then go straight to the SR-SWA architecture figure. The two components to understand are Page Gate and Token Sieve. Page Gate answers “which pages should be visible,” while Token Sieve answers “which token buckets within those pages are worth attending to.”
