It serializes multiple modalities into one sequence: RGB images, text, camera pose, depth, optical flow, and point tracks.
Key mechanisms:
- Streams of Thought: explicit multi-step sequences interleaving text/images with geometric and motion abstractions. These intermediates function as writable working memory produced by the model itself.
- Any-to-any prompting: tasks are expressed by choosing what token blocks are given vs predicted and in what order. Different orderings correspond to different inference pathways (e.g., image pair→pose; image+pose→novel view).
- Counterfactual world modeling: given a specified motion/displacement, the model predicts flow/geometry, generates the resulting scene, and then answers questions by interpreting its own predictions—reasoner and imaginer are the same model.
- RL for representation-adaptive reasoning: intermediate generations (which modalities to emit and their content) are treated as policy actions optimized end-to-end from task rewards, unlike VLM agents that call fixed external tools.
From a foundation-model angle, the most important missing-to-verify details (not present in the provided excerpt) are: tokenization/quantization of non-text modalities, mixture ratios and objectives during pretraining, and the RL stabilization constraints (e.g., KL to a reference, behavior cloning, curricula) to avoid capability collapse.b8:T5fc,The method replaces the embedding domain from the unit sphere S^{d-1} to the probability simplex Δ^{d-1}.
- Start with a frozen multimodal encoder f(·) producing pooled features h_u∈R^d.
- Add a lightweight shared adapter g_θ (linear or 2-layer MLP) to produce logits z_u.
- Two matched-capacity heads:
  (1) Euclidean/spherical head: e_u = z_u / ||z_u||_2, scored by cosine similarity.
  (2) Simplex head: p_u = softmax(z_u) ∈ Δ^{d-1}, scored by negative Total Variation distance: s_TV(u,v)=-(1/2)||p_u-p_v||_1.
- Training remains a symmetric in-batch InfoNCE (DPR-style); the only change is the output projection and the scoring function.
The paper’s argument is geometric: cosine on the sphere is invariant to rotations and sign flips, creating many equivalent solutions where cross-modal matching can be satisfied while allowing global distribution shifts between modalities. Simplex constraints (nonnegativity + unit mass) remove much of this symmetry and force both modalities to allocate probability mass over the same coordinates, effectively calibrating them. Softmax projection also introduces invariance to global logit shifts.
To isolate geometry from capacity, they compare Euclidean vs simplex using identical adapters, and further contrast an Euclidean cross-attention variant (XAttn) against ReTreever-style simplex outputs. They also introduce RelGap, a geometry-adjusted modality-gap metric that normalizes centroid separation by within-modality spread to make comparisons across domains more meaningful.b9:T7c8,The method has three main pieces. The first is the streaming interleaving format. For ASR, the sequence alternates incoming speech chunks with incremental text corresponding to words whose end times fall into each time window, with a small lookahead. For TTS, the paper compares two formats. Fixed-ratio interleaving pairs a fixed number of text tokens with a fixed number of speech frames, which is simple but poorly matched to actual acoustic boundaries. Time-aligned interleaving instead advances in words, adds word-level lookahead, and uses alignment information to define speech chunk boundaries during training. The authors choose the time-aligned version because it reduces mismatch between linguistic units and acoustic realization.

The second piece is backbone selection. Uni-Stream is built on the VibeVoice family because its TTS and ASR variants are architecturally close and, crucially, use the same speech tokenizer. That shared discrete speech space makes unification much cleaner than combining models with incompatible codecs or token inventories. The unified model is a single decoder-only LM that takes a task token followed by interleaved text and speech chunks.

The third piece is the two-stage training recipe. The authors first adapt separate TTS and ASR models to their streaming formats. Then they initialize Uni-Stream from the adapted TTS model and jointly train on both tasks. Two auxiliary objectives are introduced during unified training: synthesis anchoring, which preserves TTS quality under joint optimization, and recognition distillation, which helps the unified model acquire ASR behavior more reliably. This is a carefully asymmetric design. Starting from TTS initialization gives a strong generative prior, but ASR needs extra guidance, while joint training can still erode synthesis quality unless it is explicitly anchored. The paper also adds representation probing across tasks, modalities, and layers to study what is actually shared internally.ba:T592,The most important findings are relational rather than headline numbers. First, in streaming TTS adaptation, time-aligned interleaving yields lower TTS WER than fixed-ratio interleaving, which justifies the final data format choice. Second, the unified model reaches performance comparable to task-specific streaming models on both ASR and TTS, which is the central empirical claim: unification does not lead to a large collapse in either direction. Third, ablations show that the training recipe matters. Removing synthesis anchoring hurts TTS preservation; removing recognition distillation weakens ASR learning. Fourth, on the data side, the transcript-voting plus word-level alignment pipeline retains roughly 40,000 hours of Emilia-EN after filtering, and the authors plan to release voted transcripts and word timestamps for multiple corpora. Fifth, the probing results show that speech and text representations remain distinct across layers, while ASR and TTS representations are closer in lower layers and separate in upper layers. That result is more informative than a pure benchmark table because it explains how shared parameters can coexist with task specialization.

The paper is not centered on extreme scale. If you want to go deeper, the appendix on alignment and boundary handling is worth reading because reproducibility of time-aligned streaming TTS depends heavily on those details.bc:T8f4,The model uses a shared 24-layer bidirectional Transformer backbone with model dimension 512. Inputs are converted into token-level embeddings, processed jointly, mean-pooled, projected to a 768-dimensional embedding, and L2-normalized. Text uses a standard embedding table. Images, video, and audio are each mapped by modality-specific encoders into soft token embeddings that enter the same shared backbone. This is the key difference from classic dual-tower retrieval models: mixed-modal inputs can interact inside the sequence model before pooling.

A central architectural change is the simplified per-layer embedding design. Gemma-style PLE normally uses an additional token lookup table to inject input-conditioned residual information into each layer. Here, the model reuses the main input embeddings and modality encoder outputs instead of maintaining a separate PLE lookup table. Each layer applies a layer-specific projection, normalization, and gating mechanism to inject this information. The ablations indicate that this simplification is not merely cheaper; it also works better for this embedding setting.

Training follows a three-stage curriculum. The early stage emphasizes text-only learning to stabilize language and code representations. Later stages introduce multimodal tasks and broader domains. Distillation from Gemini Embedding 2 is separated from contrastive and regularization objectives: the model first inherits a strong global embedding geometry from the teacher, then undergoes contrastive fine-tuning to adapt the space to its own architecture and retrieval behavior. This separation is important. Pure distillation can preserve teacher structure, but it may overconstrain the student space; contrastive adaptation gives the student a chance to optimize for its own embedding geometry.

The deployment story is also part of the method. The shared backbone is only 271M parameters; adding vision yields 439M, adding audio yields 577M, and the full model is 744M. The system supports selective encoder loading, adjustable visual token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantization-aware checkpoints. So the design target is not just benchmark quality, but a modular multimodal embedding stack that can be served under different resource budgets.bd:T757,The full model has 744M parameters: a 271M shared backbone, a 167M vision encoder, and a 305M audio encoder. The backbone has 24 layers and outputs 768-dimensional embeddings. Evaluation spans seven broad benchmark suites covering text, multilingual text, code, image, video, documents, speech, and environmental sound tasks. The headline claim is that EmbeddingGemma 2 defines a new quality-efficiency Pareto frontier across modalities, often outperforming specialist systems and models that are 2x to 12x larger.

The most useful evidence comes from the ablations. First, simplified PLE outperforms the version with a dedicated lookup table while reducing cost, suggesting that preserving an input-to-layer semantic pathway matters more than maintaining a separate PLE vocabulary. Second, reducing the visual token budget has limited impact on many tasks, but hurts document retrieval much more, which is consistent with the need for fine-grained spatial and layout information in document understanding. Third, co-training the vision encoder is important; weak adaptation or freezing degrades the shared embedding space. Fourth, contrastive fine-tuning after distillation is better than relying on distillation alone. Fifth, native audio understanding beats an ASR-then-text pipeline, indicating that non-lexical acoustic information contributes materially to embedding quality.

For counting, the authors define three overlap regimes across views: complete overlap, subset overlap, and complementary views. The first two can often be solved by simple per-view heuristics such as taking the maximum count. Complementary views cannot: the model must determine which detections correspond to the same physical object and which are unique, so cross-view deduplication becomes necessary.

For cross-view consistency, the benchmark avoids a naive “spot the difference” setup. Instead, it introduces localized edits either in regions visible from both viewpoints or in regions visible from only one viewpoint. Only the former creates a true contradiction. This tests whether the model reasons about visibility and shared evidence, rather than merely detecting image-level differences.

A third task, multi-view spatial reasoning, asks models to infer physical proximity relations by combining evidence across viewpoints. The dataset is built from real-world multi-view captures from DL3DV-10K and manually verified. The paper also adds diagnostic analyses: attribution to simple aggregation strategies, sensitivity to image order, no-image bias checks, explicit reasoning prompts, and scaling with additional views. These analyses make the benchmark useful for failure diagnosis, not just ranking.c0:T57e,The evaluation covers 12 open-weight and proprietary VLMs under an open-ended protocol. The clearest result appears in counting. Accuracy is relatively moderate on complete overlap, around 45.5%–81.5%, and on subset overlap, around 26.7%–76.7%. But on complementary views, where true cross-view integration is required, performance drops sharply to 4.5%–50.0%. This gap strongly suggests that many models do not reliably establish object correspondence across views.

The consistency task is even more revealing. Accuracy stays around 50%, essentially chance level, and models respond similarly to edits in shared regions and view-specific regions. That means they are often detecting differences without understanding whether those differences are compatible with two views of the same scene.

The auxiliary analyses add useful detail. A substantial fraction of counting outputs can be explained by simple per-view aggregation rules, indicating shortcut behavior. Sensitivity to image order suggests unstable multi-image fusion. Performance under reduced or removed visual input reveals language prior bias. Explicit reasoning prompts help only marginally, which implies the bottleneck is not merely missing chain-of-thought at decoding time; it is more likely a representational failure to bind observations into a coherent scene model. Adding more views does not consistently fix the issue either.c1:T8b7,方法名是 DiFuse。整体框架很克制：冻结 diffusion 和视觉编码器，不引入外部生成器，也不加辅助损失，只在 supervised fine-tuning 阶段把原生 DiT 的中间特征注入理解路径。

具体做法分三步。

第一步是特征选择。作者先做 layer-wise analysis，研究 diffusion branch 在不同层、不同去噪阶段产生的表示，哪些对空间推理最有信息量，哪些注入后对原有语义路径干扰最小。这个分析是方法成立的前提，因为 diffusion 表示不是越多越好：早期层可能过于局部、后期层可能更偏生成目标，错误选择会把噪声或无关细节带进理解分支。

第二步是空间对齐与投影。DiFuse 从 UMM 原生 DiT 中抽取中间 spatial diffusion features，把它们投影到多模态 decoder 的 hidden space，并与视觉 token 保持空间对应关系。论文反复强调 spatial correspondence，因为作者的假设不是“扩散特征提供额外语义”，而是它们提供局部结构线索。如果在 token 对齐时打乱空间位置，收益会明显下降，这一点后面也被 feature shuffling 实验证实。

第三步是注入方式。作者不是直接替换视觉 token，也不是全层强融合，而是在选定的 decoder 层通过 residual adapters 把 diffusion 特征加到 visual-token states 上。这样做的目的，是把 diffusion 表示当作补充通道，而不是主导通道，尽量避免破坏原有 semantic pathway。论文特别关心 injection position：注入太早可能扰乱语义建模，太晚则来不及影响推理。作者通过系统分析找到干扰较小、收益较高的层位。

从方法取舍上看，DiFuse 和几类相关路线有明显区别。它不同于外接 geometry module 的方法，因为没有单独结构分支；不同于 auxiliary generation/reconstruction objective，因为没有额外训练目标；也不同于 test-time 先生成再理解的 pipeline，因为它直接复用 native diffusion states，而不是把生成过程当中间步骤。它更像一种表示重用与接口设计问题：在统一模型内部，把原本只服务生成的中间状态变成理解时可调用的结构先验。c2:T990,DiFuse is deliberately lightweight. The diffusion branch and visual encoder are kept frozen. No external generator is introduced, and no auxiliary loss is added. During supervised fine-tuning, intermediate features from the model’s native diffusion transformer are injected into the understanding pathway.

The method has three main components.

First, feature selection. The authors perform a systematic layer-wise analysis over diffusion representations from different layers and denoising stages. The goal is to identify which states are informative for spatial reasoning and which can be integrated with minimal disruption to the original semantic pathway. This matters because diffusion features are not uniformly useful: some may be too local, some too generation-specific, and naive fusion can easily inject noise.

Second, spatial alignment and projection. DiFuse extracts intermediate spatial features from the native DiT, projects them into the hidden space of the multimodal decoder, and aligns them with visual tokens while preserving spatial correspondence. This is central to the paper’s hypothesis. The benefit is not supposed to come from generic extra capacity, but from transferring local structural cues. If spatial correspondence is broken, the gains should disappear, and the paper later tests exactly that.

Third, injection via residual adapters. Instead of replacing visual tokens or performing heavy fusion throughout the network, the method injects diffusion features into visual-token states at selected decoder layers using residual adapters. This treats diffusion states as a complementary channel rather than a dominant one, helping preserve the original semantic pathway. Injection position is a major design variable: too early may interfere with semantic abstraction, too late may be too weak to affect reasoning. The paper uses empirical analysis to find favorable insertion points.

Relative to related work, DiFuse differs from geometry-augmented multimodal models because it does not add a dedicated structural module; it differs from auxiliary generation/reconstruction approaches because it does not change the training objective; and it differs from generate-then-reason pipelines because it directly reuses native diffusion states rather than using generation as an intermediate procedure. The method is best understood as an interface design for internal representation transfer within a unified model.c3:T82d,Experiments are centered on UniWorld-V1, with transfer validation on OmniGen2. The main result is that DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while keeping general multimodal performance broadly comparable.

The empirical evidence is organized around four themes.

First, main-task improvements. The paper reports gains on spatially grounded reasoning tasks after adding DiFuse. The excerpt provided does not include exact numbers, so the tables in the full paper are needed for precise margins, but the qualitative claim is clear: the spatial gains are not obtained by obviously sacrificing broad multimodal competence.

Second, ablations on feature and layer selection. The authors compare diffusion features from different layers, different denoising stages, and different decoder injection positions. This is one of the most important parts of the paper because it answers which diffusion states are actually useful. The results indicate that usefulness is selective rather than monotonic: not every layer helps, and there is a clear sweet spot for injection.

Third, tests of spatial correspondence. Feature shuffling or position perturbation substantially weakens or removes the gains, showing that the improvement depends on preserving alignment between diffusion features and visual tokens. This supports the claim that the transferred signal is structural and spatial, not just an extra source of generic features.

Fourth, transfer across architectures. Similar trends on OmniGen2 suggest that the effect is not a one-off trick tied to a single model, but a more general property of unified architectures with native diffusion branches.

For a foundation-model reader, the most useful aspect is the experimental logic. The paper does not treat diffusion features as a black-box add-on; it uses layer selection, injection-position studies, and shuffling controls to argue that native generative states carry reusable spatial structure. 1) Identify localization heads: within Qwen3.5-4B’s full-attention layers (128 heads), find a small subset that performs evidence selection. Causal importance is validated via head ablations (ablating four localization heads hurts much more than four random heads).
2) Supervise at fact tokens inside the chain: instead of supervising attention at the final answer, apply supervision at the token positions where the model states a visual fact (e.g., when predicting the object word in “the kite is blue”). This matches the observation that perception happens when facts are written, and that attention fades later.
3) Contrastive box-based attention loss: using grounding boxes, train those heads to attend more to the evidence region than to an equal-area background. The loss is formulated as an evidence-vs-background ratio so the softmax normalizer cancels, emphasizing where attention goes rather than how much total visual attention is used.
The same auxiliary loss is used in both SFT (on the model’s own correct trajectories) and GRPO-style outcome RL (on correct rollouts). A gradient decomposition is used to argue outcome rewards select trajectories, while the attention term provides a consistent routing gradient. - Define the energy in a latent space instead of pixel space to reduce effective sampling dimensionality and improve mixing.
- Use a ViT-style transformer as the energy network, with modern stability-oriented components (RoPE, QK normalization, SwiGLU, RMSNorm/AdaLN-like conditioning) rather than classic EBM-specific constraints like spectral normalization.
- Multi-layer energy extraction: read out energies from multiple transformer layers and sum them, so different depths impose complementary constraints (local texture vs global semantics), reducing the burden on a single scalar head.
- Train with a contrastive / approximate maximum-likelihood gradient: positives from data, negatives from the model’s own short-run Langevin dynamics, using persistent chains initialized from Gaussian noise.
- Sampling/training engineering: step-size vs noise tuning, persistent buffers, and explicit latent/representation alignment choices to make high-res training workable.

First, representation unification. The paper introduces an Everything-as-RGB scheme: depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow are each mapped into a three-channel image-like sequence. These are then encoded by the same frozen video autoencoder used for RGB video. The motivation is straightforward: reuse the pretrained video latent space instead of introducing modality-specific encoders and decoders. The trade-off is that non-RGB modalities are forced through an RGB-like interface, so the burden is on experiments to show that important geometric structure is preserved.

Second, architectural unification. A shared Video DiT backbone handles all modalities, with lightweight task modulation providing task-specific conditioning. The transformer blocks and decoder remain shared, and the design explicitly avoids modality-specific output heads. Compared with standard multi-task systems, this is a stronger form of parameter sharing. The upside is tighter cross-task coupling and less architectural fragmentation. The downside is a higher risk of task interference, especially because generation and perception may prefer different internal representations.

Third, objective-space unification. All tasks are trained in a common velocity prediction space, following the native v-prediction formulation of diffusion models. Instead of attaching separate regression or classification heads for perception, the model learns all modalities through the same denoising-style prediction framework. At inference time, the model supports two modes: iterative future video generation with aligned dense outputs, and single-step dense perception from an observed video without full denoising rollout.

The important point is that the paper is not merely doing multi-task learning on top of a video generator. It is trying to show that generation and perception can coexist inside one shared latent dynamics model, with a common prediction formulation.cb:T651,From the provided full-text excerpt, the evaluation spans diverse embodied settings, including multiple robot embodiments, human-hand interactions, and unseen tasks. The paper claims strong performance in both future video generation and dense perception, together with systematic design ablations. The excerpt does not include the full numerical tables, so the exact gains cannot be quoted here, but the experimental structure is still clear.

The first goal is to test whether joint modeling improves over a generate-then-estimate pipeline, especially in alignment and temporal consistency of dense outputs. The second is to verify that the three-way unification matters: shared backbone versus modality-specific heads, unified velocity prediction versus separate task objectives, and lightweight modulation versus more fragmented architectures. The third is to confirm that the same model is useful in both inference regimes: multi-step future imagination and single-step perception on observed videos.

The main empirical claim is reciprocal transfer. Video generation contributes strong spatiotemporal priors that help dense perception, while supervision from geometry, semantics, and motion pushes the shared backbone toward more physically meaningful representations. When reading the full paper, the most informative ablations to inspect are the ones that remove task modulation, reintroduce separate heads, or replace the unified velocity objective with task-specific losses. First, the authors build a controlled set of moral dilemmas from four classic works in PG19 instead of relying on synthetic dilemmas. Gemma-4 31B extracts a situational premise P and two competing duty assertions D1 and D2. A Z3 SMT solver verifies that P∧D1 is satisfiable, P∧D2 is satisfiable, and P∧D1∧D2 is unsatisfiable. This filters out cases where a trivial compromise would satisfy both duties. Out of 185 raw candidates, 156 pass all three checks. Second, each dilemma is paired with five ethical lenses: Kantian deontology, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, care ethics, and social contract theory, yielding 780 training prompts. The policy is initialized from instruction-tuned Gemma-4 E4B, described as 4.5B effective parameters and 8B total parameters. For each prompt, it generates 8 completions with a separated thinking block and visible answer. Third, rewards come from a self-judged tournament. The same policy judges its own completions pairwise using a prompt based on Wachsmuth’s 15-dimensional argument-quality taxonomy. It reasons over the dimensions but emits four preferences: logic, rhetoric, dialectic, and overall quality. The overall preference is used as the reward. All 28 pairs among 8 completions are judged in both presentation orders, producing 56 judgments per prompt. Presentation flips are treated as ties. Because ties are explicit, the authors use a Rao-Kupper preference model rather than a plain Bradley-Terry model, then convert latent strengths into RLOO advantages. Masked thinking restricts the policy gradient to visible answer tokens. Compared with scalar outcome rewards or label-only moral training, this setup directly optimizes relative argument quality while controlling for trivial compromise and order bias.cd:T47b,The experiments address judge reliability, training dynamics, and transfer. First, the self-judge’s argument-quality preferences broadly align with human annotators. The policy becomes more decisive, uses more forward-looking obligations, and relies less on caveats and retrospective justification. This is not merely a data movement issue. It determines which trajectories enter training, when they become visible to the optimizer, and how stale the policy becomes before updated parameters reach rollout workers. The paper isolates two coupled problems. First, batch-level admission constraints—such as source-mixture ratios and partial-rollout completion quotas—create a train-batch admission barrier if the system waits for a full train batch before admitting any data. In disaggregated execution, this adds extra parameter-version lag beyond ordinary off-policy delay, which the authors call architectural staleness. Second, trajectory payloads are large and heterogeneous: token IDs, per-token auxiliary metadata, and multimodal inputs. Existing sample-centric storage and retrieval do not match the actual consumption pattern of distributed training, causing redundant reads, unnecessary transfers, and serialized preparation on the critical path. The paper asks how to preserve RL training constraints while making this handoff both fresher and faster.d0:T413,This is not a pretraining paper in the narrow sense, but it is relevant to anyone working on large-scale online training. Its main contribution is conceptual as much as practical. It separates algorithmic staleness from system-induced architectural staleness and shows that admission policy alone can materially change learning quality under the same RL algorithm. That matters for RLHF, reasoning RL, online data generation, and any future setting where training consumes freshly produced data rather than a static corpus. A second contribution is methodological: the paper does not treat throughput as the only systems metric. It connects freshness, feasibility of batch composition, topology-aware data access, and multimodal encoder reuse into one coordinated pipeline. In terms of impact, this looks like a strong systems paper rather than a new optimization method: it does not change the RL objective, but it reduces the quality gap between disaggregated and colocated training at very large model scales and under multimodal workloads.d1:T80c,KnitTrans has three tightly connected components. (1) Constraint-preserving mini-batch admission. Instead of waiting until an entire train batch satisfies all batch-wide constraints, the system admits mini-batches early. The difficulty is feasibility: early admission from faster sources can consume too much capacity and make the final train batch impossible to complete under source quotas or rollout-progress requirements. To address this, the paper introduces progressive readiness targets and feasibility guards. Progressive targets allow early mini-batches to deviate from the final train-batch composition, as long as rollout progress reaches a gradually tightening target. Feasibility guards check, at each admission step, whether the remaining capacity is still sufficient to satisfy all unmet quotas. This is the key mechanism that breaks the admission barrier without violating end-of-batch constraints. (2) On-demand trajectory data access. The paper argues that sample-level storage is a poor fit for distributed RL training. It stores trajectory payloads as independently addressable atomic units, then reorganizes access according to the actual training topology. Tensor-parallel ranks share inputs, context-parallel ranks consume sequence slices, and multimodal encoders may have different placement from the backbone. Therefore, data should be fetched at the granularity required by each consumer, not by sample boundaries. After admission, retrieval, packing, and delivery proceed incrementally in micro-batch consumption order and overlap with computation. (3) Multimodal encoding deduplication. In GRPO-style RL, multiple trajectories often share the same multimodal input. Shared storage alone does not remove repeated encoder forward passes during training. KnitTrans encodes each unique multimodal input once per mini-batch, reuses the representation across all consuming trajectories, and accumulates their gradients for the encoder update. The novelty is not a single formula but a coordinated redesign of the rollout-to-training path.d2:T569,Experiments are run on a 256-GPU cluster with models ranging from 235B to 671B total parameters. 从机制上看，ST 是最有意思的配置。它让历史由 student rollout 产生，因此能覆盖 student 真正会到达的状态；但当前动作前缀由 teacher 生成，因此 teacher 在 token 级监督时仍处在自己熟悉、连贯的局部轨迹上，不会被 student 的错误 prefix 绑死。相反，SS 虽然最“on-policy”，但 teacher 需要在 student 已经写偏的动作前缀后继续给监督，这时监督信号可能变得不自然、低熵或不稳定。TS 通常介于两者之间：历史仍是 teacher-clean 的，但动作前缀来自 student，已经引入局部偏移。作者还进一步研究 mixture 和 schedule：不是固定选一种配置，而是在固定预算下混合多种配置，并比较相同 on-policy 比例但不同配对方式的效果；再进一步比较前期偏 TT、后期再引入 SS 的动态课程是否优于静态混合。d5:T852,The proposed framework, hierarchical agent distillation, factorizes context generation into two binary choices: history source H∈{T,S} and action-prefix source A∈{T,S}. This yields four configurations: TT (teacher history, teacher prefix), ST (student history, teacher prefix), TS (teacher history, student prefix), and SS (student history, student prefix). The student always learns to match the teacher’s next-token distribution on the resulting context (h, u), but the way (h, u) is constructed differs across configurations.

The key contribution is not just enumerating four cases. It disentangles three design decisions that are usually conflated: where to follow the student, how much each source configuration should contribute, and whether that allocation should change over training. To control confounders, the authors use self-distillation: teacher and student start from the same checkpoint, the teacher is frozen, and only the teacher receives privileged task guidance unavailable to the student at deployment. This removes differences in architecture, scale, and initialization, so the comparison isolates the effect of context distribution.

Mechanistically, ST is the most interesting case. Student-generated histories expose the teacher to the states the student actually reaches, which improves corrective supervision. But teacher-generated action prefixes keep token-level supervision on coherent local continuations, avoiding the situation where the teacher must continue from a malformed student prefix. SS is fully on-policy, but that is exactly why it can be weak: the teacher is queried on contexts that may already be locally broken. TS sits in between: the global state is clean, but the local token prefix is student-induced and can still degrade supervision quality.

The paper then studies mixtures and schedules. Instead of committing to one configuration, it mixes TT/ST/TS/SS under a fixed budget and compares mixtures with the same aggregate amount of student-generated data but different pairings. It also studies dynamic allocation over training, such as front-loading TT and delaying SS.d6:T6e8,The experiments are organized into three stages. Stage 1 evaluates the four configurations in isolation to separate the effects of history source and action-prefix source. The main result is consistent: ST is generally the strongest standalone configuration, while SS is the weakest across the tested settings. This supports the paper’s central claim that student histories and student prefixes have very different roles.

Stage 2 studies mixed training. A useful result here is that one cannot summarize a mixture by a single “on-policy fraction.” Two mixtures can have the same proportion of student-generated histories and student-generated prefixes, yet perform differently depending on how those sources are paired across TT/ST/TS/SS. The best tested mixtures emphasize hybrid configurations, especially ST, while retaining some TT and a small amount of SS. The role of SS is subtle: it is weak on its own, but a modest allocation can still help in a mixture by exposing the student to fully deployment-like rollouts.

Stage 3 studies timing. Front-loading TT improves early learning because teacher-clean contexts are easier and more stable. Delaying SS improves later and final validation performance because fully on-policy exposure becomes more useful once the student has acquired some competence. A schedule combining both effects outperforms static allocation.

First, Relative Visual Encoding defines a context-relative visual coordinate rather than using raw image affinity. It contrasts a predictive state’s cosine affinity to image representations against its affinity to prompt-background representations, under a shared diagonal scaling. This is meant to capture whether a token is relatively more image-driven than context-driven. Second, Outcome-conditioned Evidence Calibration combines that visual coordinate with predictive features and estimates their evidential contribution from contrasts between positive- and negative-advantage responses. The key idea is that visual relevance does not automatically imply stronger updates; contribution should depend on outcome-conditioned separation and variance-aware calibration. The paper explicitly notes that if the positive and negative sides have the same visual reference mean, the visual term should contribute zero. Third, Normalized Credit Allocation converts calibrated evidence into positive, globally normalized token coefficients that modulate the original sequence advantage while preserving its sign. 1) Empirical sufficiency of behavior traces: an external estimator trained only on (question, response, correctness) triples—without access to the policy’s hidden states—can match a self-estimator of comparable capacity trained on the same supervision. This suggests confidence is largely identifiable from observable behavior.
2) Formal equivalence to RL value learning: define confidence as the conditional probability of a correct final outcome given the information available along the generation trajectory (question + generated prefix). In RL terms, this is a value function V(s)=E[return|state]. With binary correctness reward, V(s) is the probability of eventual correctness; with continuous quality rewards, V(s) is expected quality.
Algorithmically, Critic-as-Confidence (CaC) reuses the RL critic trained during PPO as the confidence estimator. For critic-free RL variants (the paper mentions GRPO), they fit a value model post hoc on rollouts and use it similarly. Because the critic can be queried at intermediate prefixes, CaC provides step-/prefix-level confidence, enabling early termination and confidence-guided decoding/selection.da:T691,PRISM has two coupled components. First, it constructs multi-solution supervision with submodular curation. For each prompt, the system gathers candidate solutions from multiple teachers and selects a subset that is both correct and diverse in terms of reasoning-feature coverage. The important point is that diversity is defined semantically, not lexically: trajectories are mapped to discrete reasoning features, and the selected subset maximizes coverage rather than surface variation. Second, the model is trained and sampled with Gaussian noise injected into a small set of special-token embeddings. Without curated multi-solution supervision, this would behave like ordinary embedding noise. With that supervision, however, different noise draws become learned latent routing signals that steer generation toward different valid trajectories.

The theoretical analysis interprets the perturbation as a stable regularizer on the Hessian of the loss with respect to embeddings, under small-noise assumptions. That helps explain why the method does not rely on aggressive stochasticity. The design choice is also deliberate: perturbing special-token embeddings is cheaper and more localized than injecting noise broadly into hidden states or logits, and it creates a consistent train-test interface. Relative to prior work, PRISM differs from inference-time diversity methods because it does not force variation only at decoding time; it differs from generic noise regularization because the noise is paired with explicit multi-mode supervision; and it differs from plain multi-solution SFT because it adds a mechanism for controllable mode selection within the learned support.db:T5e1,The evaluation has three parts. Concretely, it brings two vectors into the same actor-logit space at each position t:
- Reward direction g_t: an end-to-end surrogate gradient of the frozen reward model’s score w.r.t. the actor logits for the sampled response. Because tokens are discrete, the method uses a straight-through surrogate to backpropagate through the sampled tokens into the reward model and then back into the actor’s logit space.
- Policy update direction k_t: the gradient direction that increases the probability of the sampled token (log-prob gradient). GRPO’s response-level advantage A determines whether the update reinforces (A>0) or suppresses (A<0) that sampled action direction.

Directional credit is then d_t = ⟨g_t, k_t⟩. Under a local first-order approximation, this inner product predicts whether moving along the GRPO-induced direction will increase reward locally at that token. DATC converts this into token weights by redistributing the response-level advantage across positions using a softmax over A d / τ, producing a token-level advantage while preserving the overall sign structure. A KL regularizer constrains deviation from vanilla GRPO.

The paper also provides a theoretical link: the end-to-end surrogate gradient can be written in an advantage-weighted form consistent with REINFORCE, and d_t can be interpreted as aggregating local advantages from a linearized reward model along the sampled-action direction.dd:T601,The technical contribution has three layers. First, the paper reframes the notion of knowledge in OPD. Standard OPD samples trajectories from the student and minimizes reverse KL to a frozen teacher at every token. Existing analyses mostly track Overlap@k, the agreement between student and teacher top-k token sets, which captures only how to branch. The authors introduce entropy shape: the sequence of next-token entropies along a trajectory. High-entropy positions correspond to forks where the model keeps options open; low-entropy positions correspond to committed continuation. This gives a concrete representation of where to branch. Second, they define Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC), which measures alignment between student and teacher entropy shapes on the same trajectory. ESC is about the positional pattern of uncertainty, not token identity. Third, they provide both observational and causal evidence that this signal matters. Observationally, in successful OPD runs, ESC rises during training together with student performance; in unsuccessful runs, ESC starts high and quickly plateaus, suggesting little remaining uncertainty gap to learn from. Causally, they build counterfactual teachers by transplanting the entropy shape of one teacher onto another while preserving token preferences as much as possible. This isolates where to branch from how to branch. The resulting experiments show that a successful teacher’s entropy shape alone can improve distillation, and that ESC can change independently of Overlap@k.de:T59f,The experiments are designed to validate mechanism rather than maximize benchmark scores. First, example selection. EVAN estimates scaled image information gain (scaled-IIG) for each training instance, measuring how much the image contributes to answer correctness. Only visually dependent examples are selected for intervention, which avoids injecting noise into cases that can already be solved from language alone. To prevent the selected pool from collapsing into a narrow subset of tasks, the paper uses a mixed-ranking strategy that balances visual dependence with data diversity.

Second, evidence ablation. For each selected example, the method identifies query-critical image patches that support the verified response. These patches are then masked to create an evidence-ablated image. The key design choice is that the perturbation is not coarse or task-agnostic; it removes exactly the visual evidence that keeps the answer grounded. Sampling from the current policy on this ablated image tends to produce responses that remain fluent and plausible, but are now visually ungrounded. These become EVAN’s hard negatives.

Third, RL optimization. The negatives are not optimized under the ablated image. Instead, they are brought back under the clean image condition, so the model is explicitly trained to suppress language-prior failures when the relevant evidence is actually available. The training recipe includes several stabilization mechanisms: filtering out low-probability or overly long ablated responses, bounding negative advantages so negatives do not dominate the update, and combining the method with DAPO-style clipping and dynamic sampling for stable long-form reasoning optimization. Compared with prior multimodal RL methods that use image perturbations, the main difference is that EVAN treats perturbation as a tool for constructing informative negatives, not as the end objective.e1:T5fe,The experimental story is not just about end-task accuracy; it is also about grounding behavior. On a set of challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks, EVAN improves over standard RLVR/GRPO baselines, with larger gains on subsets where visual evidence is more necessary. That pattern matches the method design: it is meant to correct language shortcuts, not to uniformly help every example.

The ablations are the most informative part. Removing scaled-IIG-based selection and applying evidence ablation to all samples hurts performance, showing that visually dependent example selection is necessary. Replacing query-critical masking with random masking or coarse perturbations produces weaker negatives and worse downstream gains, which supports the claim that negative quality matters more than perturbation quantity. The stability ablations are also important: without plausibility filtering or bounded negative advantages, training becomes less stable, indicating that the method is not simply “add negative rewards and hope for the best.”

与已有 adaptive OPSD 的区别有两层。第一，适配粒度从 response-level 变成 token-level。第二，选择对象不只是“参考答案暴露多少”，而是从多个 teacher 中动态选一个最适合当前位置的 teacher。方法上仍属于蒸馏框架，没有引入复杂 RL credit assignment，也没有训练额外 gating 网络；这使它实现上相对直接，但也意味着计算成本主要来自多 teacher 前向和 token 级选择逻辑。e7:T895,The paper first runs a teacher-intervention pilot study to test whether token-level teacher preference is real. The setup is simple but well targeted: keep a student-generated prefix, let a candidate teacher take over for a short continuation at a selected token position, then hand control back to the student to finish the response. The final accuracy gain of this student-teacher-student relay over pure student generation is used as a proxy for teacher suitability at that token position. This matters because it measures whether local teacher intervention actually improves the end result, rather than only comparing static distributional distances.

Motivated by that study, the authors propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation, or MTA-OPSD. Instead of one teacher, the method builds a pool of candidate teachers by varying how much of the privileged reference is exposed and how it is truncated. This creates teachers with different information content and different sharpness levels. During training, each token in a student rollout selects its own teacher from this pool. The selection procedure uses majority voting to identify a reliable subset of candidate teachers, followed by KL-based selection to pick the preferred teacher for that token.

The paper claims that the preferred teacher tends to have a large student-teacher KL distance. That is somewhat counterintuitive at first glance, since large KL is often associated with mismatch. The intended interpretation seems to be that, once majority voting filters out unreliable candidates, a larger KL can indicate a more informative corrective signal rather than an unhelpful overconfident one.

Relative to prior adaptive OPSD methods, the novelty has two parts. First, adaptation moves from the response level to the token level. Second, the model does not merely tune one teacher’s reference exposure; it dynamically chooses among multiple teachers for each token. The framework remains within distillation rather than RL, and it does not appear to require a separate learned gating network. The practical cost is therefore likely to come from maintaining a teacher pool and performing token-level selection.e8:T67a,From the provided content, the experiments are run on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family. For pretraining-focused readers, the main takeaway is the granularity of supervision matching rather than the specific math setup.ea:T7df,PIVOT can be summarized as online local correction followed by student continuation, plus KL supervision on the corrected span. During training, the student first generates a rollout prefix. At a chosen intervention point, the teacher produces a correction conditioned on that student-generated prefix. The student then continues generation from the corrected context rather than from its original mistaken continuation. This produces teacher-assisted trajectories that are more likely to end in verifier-approved solutions, while still preserving part of the student’s own rollout distribution. That is a key difference from simply injecting full teacher trajectories.

The optimization has two coupled parts. First, the resulting trajectories are still optimized with the standard RLVR objective, instantiated with GRPO and verifier-based rewards. This keeps the training target anchored to task correctness rather than pure imitation. Second, a teacher-student KL loss is applied only on the correction segments, providing dense token-level supervision exactly where the teacher intervened. Instead of distilling the entire sequence, the method concentrates supervision on the local regions that are most responsible for steering the trajectory back toward a valid reasoning path.

Mechanistically, the method addresses both bottlenecks at once. Online intervention changes the rollout distribution and increases access to reward-bearing trajectories. Local KL makes those interventions learnable by turning them into parameter updates the student can reproduce later. The paper further studies practical design choices: where intervention should happen, how much teacher guidance to inject, and how the KL term should be used. A recurring conclusion is that too-early intervention risks turning training into teacher-led generation, while too-late intervention cannot rescue already broken trajectories. Either intervention alone or token supervision alone is often insufficient; the combination is the point.eb:T63e,The evaluation covers two hard reasoning settings: logic games from SynLogic and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing on the math side. The headline result is on hard logic games, where RL-only training makes limited progress: PIVOT improves mean avg@8 from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%, close to a 2x gain. That is a meaningful result because it directly targets the sparse-reward regime where standard RLVR tends to stall.

The most informative ablations are not just score comparisons but mechanism tests. The authors isolate trajectory-level intervention and token-level supervision, showing that each one alone can still fail to produce strong learning. Their combination gives the strongest gains, which directly supports the paper’s framing. They also study intervention placement and the KL design, showing that teacher correction is not simply “more is better.” The intervention has to occur at a point where the student can still continue productively, while being early enough to change the probability of eventual success. On mathematical reasoning tasks, PIVOT consistently beats the evaluated baselines on both ID and OOD benchmarks, suggesting that the gains are not limited to a single synthetic logic environment.

The strongest part of the empirical section is the controlled decomposition of why the method works. The paper does more than report a better final number; it shows that changing the trajectory distribution and densifying the local learning signal solve different pieces of the RLVR failure mode.ec:T5b8,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main method figure. The key idea is the decomposition of teacher guidance into two roles: improving access to successful trajectories and making those corrections learnable at the token level. Then jump to the main results table and the ablations that compare intervention-only, supervision-only, and the combined method.

For a closer read, focus on three parts. First, the formal definition of teacher-assisted trajectories and exactly how the correction-span KL is applied; this is where PIVOT differs from full teacher rollouts or sequence-level online distillation. If the goal is to judge whether this can scale to larger reasoning RL settings, those experiments matter more than the headline benchmark numbers.

Two follow-up questions are worth keeping in mind while reading. One is whether intervention position and correction length could be chosen adaptively rather than by fixed rules. The other is whether the teacher must be substantially stronger than the student, or whether committee teachers or self-improving teachers could play the same role. For anyone interested in the pretrain-to-posttrain interface, the main thing to watch is the long-term tension between verifier rewards and localized KL supervision.ed:T91d,The method builds on on-policy distillation and paired-model contrastive supervision. Let the student be an autoregressive policy πθ. The model first samples its own response y from prompt x, so training happens on the state distribution the student actually visits. Standard OPD would query a teacher πT on those states and train the student toward the teacher distribution, often with reverse KL. WISD replaces the external teacher with a pair derived from the same model: the original model serves as the stronger branch π+, and a weakened copy serves as the weaker branch π−. The training signal comes from their log-probability contrast on the same on-policy states, indicating which tokens the original model prefers more strongly than its weakened counterpart.

Conceptually, this is close to policy-shift supervision in DOPD-style methods. The goal is not merely to imitate a teacher distribution, but to extract a direction of improvement from the relative preferences of a model pair. This has two practical advantages. First, the supervision is dense across every token on the student’s own trajectories, which is useful for reasoning where intermediate steps matter. Second, because the strong and weak models share the same origin, the distribution gap may be easier to transfer than in privileged-information self-distillation, where the teacher is conditioned on extra context unavailable to the student.

The paper studies two training-free ways to construct the weaker model. One is low-bit quantization, which introduces systematic precision loss in the weights. The other is magnitude pruning, which removes low-magnitude parameters and reduces effective capacity. Both are cheap, require no calibration data, and can be applied directly to the original model. That design choice is important: the whole pipeline only needs unlabeled prompts.

The method relies on a meaningful assumption: the difference between the original model and its weakened copy should encode a stable capability drop, so that moving against that drop becomes a useful learning direction. Quantization and pruning are sensible choices because they induce structured degradation rather than arbitrary noise. If the weakening were too distorted, the contrast could reflect random perturbation instead of a usable improvement signal.ee:T655,The experiments cover multiple reasoning architectures and scales, with benchmarks in mathematical and coding reasoning. The headline numbers are strong and broad rather than isolated. Quantization-based WISD improves average accuracy by 4.0 points and yields positive gains in 21 of 25 model–benchmark settings. Pruning-based WISD improves average accuracy by 5.5 points and yields gains in 23 of 25 settings.

The paper highlights several concrete results. With pruning, Qwen3.5-4B improves from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. With quantization, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improves from 68.5% to 74.6% on HMMT 2025 and from 61.8% to 69.5% on LiveCodeBench v6. These are substantial gains for a setting that uses no privileged information.

The broader experimental story appears to test robustness across model families, task types, and weakening mechanisms, while contrasting WISD with self-distillation methods that require reference solutions or environment feedback. One practical point stands out: the weak model construction needs no calibration data, so the method is lightweight to deploy on top of an existing model.

Two caveats are worth keeping in mind while reading the results. First, the evidence is concentrated on reasoning benchmarks, so it does not automatically imply gains on open-domain chat, knowledge-heavy tasks, or long-horizon agents. Second, the true ceiling of the method likely depends on details such as trajectory quality, sampling settings, and weakening strength. Those details usually live in the ablations and appendix rather than the headline table.ef:T43c,Start with the introduction and the first half of the method section. If you want to reproduce it, read the appendix for hyperparameters, sampling settings, quantization bit-widths, and pruning ratios.f0:T49f,CoCA samples two kinds of rollouts from the same policy: query-only responses and rubric-conditioned responses. It then compares criterion-level satisfaction across the two groups to estimate where the policy currently stands. If query-only responses already satisfy a criterion, the criterion is becoming less useful for learning. If rubric-conditioned responses satisfy it while query-only responses do not, the behavior can be elicited but has not yet been internalized. If neither group satisfies it, the criterion may be beyond the current exploration frontier. CoCA uses this diagnosis to recalibrate criterion difficulty while preserving the intended evaluation target. For policy learning, it does not rely only on scalar rubric rewards. A conditioned response is treated as a guided frontier only when it satisfies the diagnosed targets, and then it is used for token-level self-distillation. Otherwise, conditioned rollout optimization is used to expand the frontier before later distillation. Compared with standard rubric RL, the method adds criterion-level capability assessment. Compared with rubric evolution alone, it ties rubric updates to policy learning decisions.f1:T435,Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL) is a two-player loop:
- Judge: given (x, y), learns to discriminate whether y comes from the reference set or from the current generator’s on-policy samples, producing a “probability of being reference” score.
- Generator: optimized with RL (implemented on top of Prime-RL) to maximize the judge score.
No verifiers, no rubrics, no chain-of-thought traces—only outcome-level reference answers.
The central hypothesis is an implicit curriculum: once the generator matches superficial cues (length/format/lexical style), those cues stop separating the distributions, forcing the judge to rely on deeper task-relevant structure; stronger judges and longer co-training should therefore yield better rewards and better policies.
Key contrasts:
- vs RLVR: reward is learned from examples, not computed by a checker.
- vs frozen LLM judges: the judge is trained jointly, with a moving decision boundary.
- vs demonstration distillation / trace-based adversarial training: supervision is reference answers only, not reasoning trajectories.f2:T476,Evaluated in five settings:
1) Three “verifiable but verifier-withheld” tasks: integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation. RAL with judge-only reward improves held-out correctness and in some settings matches or exceeds training with exact rewards (including variants that augment exact rewards with a generator-sized judge).
2) Two open-ended scientific generation tasks: biomedical abstract generation from in-domain references, and NIH grant abstract generation. RAL shifts outputs toward the target reference distribution without explicitly labeling the target domain, while maintaining semantic diversity; on NIH abstracts, outputs become harder to distinguish from real references for both LLM judges and human evaluators.
Ablations emphasize: judge capacity matters; longer co-training continues to improve the generator, consistent with the curriculum narrative.
(Note: the provided full-text excerpt does not include the complete result tables and exact numbers; reporting parameter counts, dataset sizes, and deltas requires the missing experimental sections/appendix.)f3:T5eb,HRS shifts distribution matching from output calibration to hidden-state editing.
1) Formulation: for each item x, predict a categorical rating distribution p(r|x) that matches the empirical human judgment distribution, covering both ordinal and nominal label spaces.
2) Oracle residual study: assuming access to human ratings, solve for an additive hidden-state correction Δh at a chosen transformer layer such that the downstream frozen layers produce a distribution closer to humans. Empirically, (i) intervening at a single layer captures most of the attainable gain, and (ii) the set of oracle corrections is largely low-rank—most improvement is preserved in a small subspace.
3) Human-Residual Steering: learn an input-conditioned intervention without human labels at test time. A small predictor g takes the layer hidden state and the original rating logits, outputs low-dimensional coefficients a, and a learned basis B maps them to Δh = B a. Apply h' = h + Δh at that layer; keep the backbone frozen while backpropagating through the frozen downstream stack into g and B.
4) Training objective: optimize proper scoring rules on individual annotations (multiple ratings per item), with objectives tailored to ordinal vs nominal judgments to encourage calibrated distribution prediction.
5) Positioning: compared to output-level calibration, HRS can express richer, input-dependent distribution reshaping; compared to distributional fine-tuning, it is far cheaper to deploy but may have a lower ceiling.f4:T449,ATI-OPD has two main components. Adaptive Teacher Intervention first samples a full response from the student and scores it with the teacher under the same prefixes. It uses a sampled-token absolute log-probability gap, related to the K3 estimator, to measure local teacher-student disagreement. The response is split into short segments, and the earliest segment whose mean gap exceeds a threshold is selected. The preceding student prefix is kept, the divergent segment and its original suffix are discarded, and the teacher writes a bounded replacement segment. The student then continues generation from this revised prefix. Adaptive Supervision Selection monitors the regenerated continuation and removes persistently divergent suffix windows from the distillation loss. This differs from length control or token reweighting because it changes the conditional trajectory before later supervision is collected. The OPD objective remains reverse-KL-style token-level distillation, implemented with teacher log-probabilities over the student’s top-16 candidates and a clipped policy surrogate.f5:T5f0,The paper structures the study around four research questions.
- RQ1 (compositionality): test whether the activation→text mapping respects structured operations in activation space. They use analogy-style constructions on activations (e.g., verbalize(b−a+c)) to see if the resulting text reflects applying the semantic change from a→b onto c. The underlying premise is: diff verbalization is only trustworthy if the verbalizer is approximately compositional.
- RQ2 (transfer to fine-tuned models): an NLA is trained on residual-stream activations from an “original” model; diffing requires processing activations from fine-tuned descendants. They measure reconstruction fidelity (via explained-variance style metrics) on base vs fine-tuned activations to assess reuse without retraining.
- RQ3 (recover fine-tuning objectives): feed activation differences into the verbalizer and analyze which generated tokens/phrases are most informative about the fine-tuning objective. This shifts the goal from “can it generate an explanation” to “which parts of the explanation are stable signals usable for automated diff reports.”
- RQ4 (specialization for diffing): adapt training to make NLAs better at handling differences (e.g., more sensitive/structured diff descriptions), then evaluate improvements on diff-oriented metrics.
Methodologically, they favor free-form language (avoiding fixed inventories like logit lens/SAEs) and pay the price of having to empirically validate controllability and transfer.f6:T704,The paper first places seven theories into a common comparison frame: Star-free, AC0, TC0, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity. It translates their claims into a unified prediction matrix over a task suite designed to separate them, including Boolean tasks, graph problems, retrieval, and formal-language tasks such as Dyck recognition. Where the literature does not already provide the needed result, the authors add new theoretical constructions or separations.

The empirical side has two layers. One uses small task-specific transformers trained from scratch, with controlled choices such as positional encoding, to test both fitting and length generalization. The other probes frontier pretrained LLMs on related tasks. This split is important because it helps distinguish architectural expressivity from optimization barriers and from capabilities induced by large-scale pretraining.

Several concrete comparisons are especially informative. Theories based on hard attention cannot express global aggregation, so they predict tasks like Majority to be hard; in practice, transformers can learn them and sometimes length-generalize. C-RASP captures global aggregation by modeling attention as uniform averaging, but it misses content-dependent retrieval; the paper proves an exponential-size requirement for C-RASP on a retrieval task that softmax-attention transformers solve efficiently, and observes the same qualitative gap empirically. In the other direction, theories based on loose circuit upper bounds or communication-style abstractions with unbounded local computation predict many tasks to be feasible even when trained transformers fail to learn them. The broader message is that each theory tends to fail exactly where performance depends on a feature omitted by its abstraction.f7:T497,The main empirical findings are straightforward. First, no single theory explains the full behavior of either small transformers or frontier LLMs. Second, hard predictions are much more trustworthy than easy predictions. Easy predictions often come from handcrafted constructions or loose upper bounds and therefore overstate what training will achieve. Third, Parity is a useful counterexample: transformers can fail even to fit the training data, which points to an optimization barrier rather than a pure expressivity limit. Fourth, positional encoding has a large effect on length generalization, and different tasks prefer different encodings; current theories mostly do not model this source of inductive bias. Fifth, pretrained LLMs behave differently from small transformers trained from scratch, implying that a theory of LLM behavior must include data and training, not architecture alone.

The paper also contributes new theoretical results to complete the prediction matrix and uses tasks such as Majority and retrieval to show where different abstractions break. The contribution is therefore more about systematic diagnosis than about a single benchmark number.f8:T928,核心做法分两段：
1) 统一的 retrieval-head 检测与跨模态对齐分析。
- 定义：对每个样本 i，有问题 token 集 Qi、证据 token 集 Gi。对每层 l、每头 h，计算从问题位置 q 到上下文位置 t 的注意力 a_lh^(i)(q,t)。
- 校准：注意力里有位置偏好/内容偏好等与“问题”无关的成分。沿用 MMRetHead 的思路，用同一上下文但把问题替换成“无信息问题”得到 u_lh^(i,∅)，用两者差异构造 calibrated retrieval score s_lh（文中给出公式），以减少“头本来就爱看某些位置/模态 token”的伪相关。
- 排序：按 s_lh 给所有头排序，默认取 top 5% 作为 retrieval heads，并在不同任务/设置下比较稀疏性与重叠度。

1) Unified retrieval-head detection with calibration.
- For each example with question tokens Q and annotated evidence tokens G, compute per-head attention from question positions to context positions.
- To remove question-independent biases (positional preferences, modality-token priors), recompute attention using an uninformative/empty question on the same context, and define a calibrated retrieval score (following MMRetHead). Heads are ranked by this score; the top 5% are treated as retrieval heads by default.

2) Controlled cross-modality setup (AV-NIAH).
- Construct paired audio-visual inputs where the evidence content is identical but presented either as synthesized speech (audio condition) or as on-screen text in a banner (visual condition), while keeping background video, insertion depth, question, and answer fixed. Map the evidence time span to the corresponding audio/video token span.
- Analyze 18 checkpoints spanning language, vision-language, unified, and omni-modal models to study head reuse and preservation during modality expansion.

3) Causal tests and optimization.
- Perform targeted head ablations to test necessity for audio-visual retrieval; additionally ablate only the subset of heads shared across modalities (reported as <2% of all heads) to test whether a compact shared circuit supports broader multimodal reasoning.
- For multimodal document retrieval (MMDocIR), select retrieval heads on document-related tasks, aggregate their question→page attention into a page score, and train it with a ranking objective to prefer relevant pages over distractors. The key idea is to treat internal attention as a trainable scorer without redesigning the whole model.fa:T49d,Key findings are organized as four analyses plus an application result:
- Sparsity: retrieval scores concentrate in a small number of heads for both spoken and displayed evidence in AV-NIAH.
- Cross-modal sharing: when the same information is delivered via audio vs on-screen text, many of the top retrieval heads overlap, indicating reuse across modalities.
- Preservation: omni-modal models largely retain retrieval heads from their language or vision-language backbones, and those retained heads remain functionally important.

A norm-matched local likelihood diagnostic suggests t2 edits increase likelihood of safe continuations and decrease unsafe ones, whereas later edits can suppress both.fc:T463,The analysis uses singular learning theory. The central quantity is the real log canonical threshold, or RLCT, which replaces half the parameter dimension in the leading asymptotics of Bayesian generalization and marginal likelihood for singular models. Under a local linearization of the pretrained network, LoRA becomes a low-rank trace-regression problem. Its KL geometry is governed by a forward-backward covariance built from input activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. If this covariance is nondegenerate on the relevant low-rank directions, the classical reduced-rank regression RLCT is recovered. If its kernel intersects those directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters appear, changing the singular geometry. The paper characterizes this locally through observable tangent directions plus a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. A notable conclusion is that the global learning complexity need not be determined by the ground-truth stratum; singularities on other rank strata can dominate the asymptotics.fd:T916,核心方法是定义并精确计算 leverage。给定锚点参数 θ0 和一个更新方向 Δ，作者考虑沿 αΔ 微小移动后，模型 next-token distribution 的 KL 变化。对 KL 做二阶展开，系数就是 Fisher 二次型 Δ^T F Δ，其中 F 是在固定评估语料上按 token 平均得到的 Fisher / Gauss-Newton 形式。作者不用有限差分，而是用一次 forward-mode Jacobian-vector product 精确算出每个方向的曲率 c(Δ)，再除以同一锚点、同一位移尺度下随机方向的平均曲率 c(null)，得到 leverage ρ = c(Δ)/c(null)。这样定义有几个优点：

1）它衡量的是“相对随机方向”的行为敏感度，而不是绝对 KL，因此能消掉参数重参数化和尺度的一部分影响；
2）它不需要真的沿方向 perturb 权重，因此没有有限差分在极小位移下的 cancellation floor；
3）它天然落在局部 Fisher 几何里，能把更新方向是否对准高敏感子空间这件事量化出来。

作者还定义了几种 null 和分解。isotropic null 给出标准 leverage；profile null 匹配各 tensor 的范数分布；sign-flip null 保持每个坐标的绝对值只随机化符号，用来分离“幅度放在哪些坐标”和“符号是否沿着正确协同方向”这两部分贡献。对应地，ρsign 可以理解为更新符号结构相对随机符号的价值，这在分析 DARE 随机丢弃并重缩放时尤其关键。

在实验设计上，作者既分析公开 released checkpoints，也做 controlled reruns。公开模型包括 OLMo-3、Tülu-3、Zephyr、OLMo-2 等多个阶段的 checkpoint。控制实验则在 0.5B 和 7B 规模上重跑 SFT 与 DPO，并严格使用 fp32 master weights，观察 leverage 如何随相对位移 relΔW 衰减。作者还重现 OLMo-2-1B 的 released DPO recipe，并做 recipe ablation，定位 leverage 水平来自哪些训练细节。

理论上，论文给出一个 noisy quadratic SGD 模型来解释为什么预训练窗口 leverage 会接近 1。直观上，在局部二次近似下，如果优化过程长期受梯度噪声驱动并在许多曲率方向上来回游走，那么累计位移虽然大，但在 Fisher 度量下并没有比随机方向更集中地对准高曲率子空间，因此单位位移带来的输出变化接近随机基线。fe:T9f2,实验结果很扎实，且数字有辨识度。

第一组结果是不同训练阶段的 leverage 地图。公开 checkpoint 上，预训练窗口在 prose 上基本落在 ρ≈1 的随机水平；SFT 大约在 5 左右；RL-Zero 和 RLVR 在 400 到 1,500；DPO 在 400 到 23,000。也就是说，后训练尤其 preference / RL 类阶段，虽然参数位移通常只有 10^-4 到 10^-3 或 10^-1 量级，但单位位移造成的输出分布变化远高于预训练。这个量级差跨了四个数量级。

第二组结果是 leverage 会沿训练轨迹被“花掉”。在作者控制的 SFT 和 DPO 训练中，无论 0.5B 还是 7B，只要从同一 anchor 往外走，ρ 都随着相对位移 relΔW 下降。SFT 的下降大致符合 relΔW^-0.7 到 relΔW^-1.7，DPO 则是 relΔW^-0.3 到 relΔW^-1.2。含义是：训练早期的更新方向更集中地对准高敏感子空间，越往后越接近把高 leverage 机会消耗完，后续更新的单位收益下降。

第三组结果是数值精度。若直接用 bf16 参数训练且没有 fp32 master copy，会冻结 36% 到 99% 的坐标，并使 leverage 最多下降 7 倍。更细一点，作者还发现这种设置会人为制造更新幅度与 diagonal Fisher 的对齐，而在 fp32 master 训练中这种对齐并不存在。这说明很多关于“更新偏向重要参数”的观察，可能部分是精度伪影，而不全是优化动力学本身。

第四组结果是 recipe 复现与归因。作者从 released SFT checkpoint 重跑 OLMo-2-1B 的 DPO recipe，能复现 released delta 的位移、leverage 和 sign structure。若换成一个更朴素的 recipe，在同一 anchor 上 leverage 会低 5 到 6 倍。进一步做 leave-one-component-out 控制，发现 length-normalized loss 和 batch size 128 共同抬高了 leverage 水平。这一点很有价值，因为它把“为什么某个 DPO delta 特别可复用”落到了具体 recipe 组件上。

第五组结果是 leverage 对 delta reuse 的预测。作者推导出 DARE 这类随机 drop-and-rescale 操作的相对损伤约为 (1-p)/(pρsign)，其中 p 是保留率。实测中，只要 DARE 适用，这个公式通常能在约两倍误差内预测性能损伤。说明 ρsign 确实抓住了 delta 可稀疏化、可合并的一部分核心结构。

另外，作者还对有限差分与精确 Fisher 二次型做了校验：在有限差分高于数值底噪的区域，两者在 659 个检查中有 649 个误差在 4% 以内。这给方法本身的可信度提供了很强支撑。ff:T430,This is highly relevant to pretraining research. First, it provides a stage-agnostic diagnostic that is more informative than raw loss decrease or parameter norm change. It directly measures whether an update direction is aligned with behaviorally sensitive directions in the local Fisher geometry. Second, the paper makes a strong claim: on prose, pretraining windows of 30k to 1M steps often have leverage near 1, meaning they are no more consequential than random directions of the same size. That changes how one might think about scaling, cooldown, continual pretraining, and the pretrain-to-post-train interface. Third, it elevates numerical precision from an implementation detail to a training-dynamics issue: bf16 training without fp32 master weights freezes many coordinates, lowers leverage substantially, and creates an apparent alignment between update magnitudes and diagonal Fisher that is absent in fp32-master training. Fourth, it connects leverage to delta reuse and gives a predictive handle on the damage induced by DARE-style drop-and-rescale merging.100:T950,The central object is leverage. Given an anchor checkpoint θ0 and an update direction Δ, the authors consider the KL divergence between the anchor model and the model moved slightly along αΔ. A second-order expansion gives a Fisher quadratic form, Δ^T F Δ, where F is the token-averaged Fisher or Gauss-Newton matrix on a fixed evaluation corpus. Instead of estimating this curvature by finite differences, they compute it exactly with a forward-mode Jacobian-vector product, yielding c(Δ). They then normalize by the average curvature of random directions of the same size at the same anchor, c(null), and define leverage as ρ = c(Δ) / c(null).

This construction has several advantages. It measures behavioral sensitivity relative to a random baseline rather than in absolute KL units. It avoids the cancellation floor that makes tiny finite-difference KL estimates unreliable. And it naturally asks whether an update is aligned with high-sensitivity subspaces of the local Fisher geometry.

The paper also introduces several null models and decompositions. The isotropic null gives the default leverage. The profile null matches tensor-wise norms. The sign-flip null keeps the coordinate magnitudes fixed and randomizes only the signs, which separates the contribution of where the update puts its magnitude from whether the signs are coordinated correctly. The resulting sign-structure leverage, ρsign, is especially useful for understanding sparsification and merge operations such as DARE.

Empirically, the authors combine released-checkpoint analysis with controlled reruns. They analyze checkpoints from OLMo-3, Tülu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 across multiple stages. They also rerun controlled SFT and DPO at 0.5B and 7B with fp32 master weights to study how leverage decays with relative displacement. In addition, they reproduce the released OLMo-2-1B DPO recipe and ablate recipe components to identify what drives high leverage.

On the theory side, they propose a noisy quadratic SGD model to explain why long pretraining windows can end up with leverage near 1. The intuition is that under a local quadratic approximation, if SGD is dominated by noise over long horizons, the accumulated displacement can become large while failing to remain preferentially aligned with high-curvature directions. In Fisher geometry, the net direction then looks close to random.101:T8a0,The empirical picture is unusually clear. Across released checkpoints, pretraining windows sit near ρ ≈ 1 on prose, essentially at the random baseline. SFT is around 5. RL-Zero and RLVR range from about 400 to 1,500. DPO ranges from about 400 to 23,000. So post-training, especially preference- and RL-style stages, buys far more output change per unit of weight movement than pretraining does, spanning roughly four orders of magnitude.

The controlled runs show that leverage is spent along the trajectory. In both SFT and DPO, at both 0.5B and 7B, leverage decays as relative displacement grows. For SFT the decay is roughly relΔW^-0.7 to relΔW^-1.7, and for DPO roughly relΔW^-0.3 to relΔW^-1.2. The interpretation is that early updates are more aligned with behaviorally sensitive directions, while later updates consume that opportunity and become less efficient per unit displacement.

The precision experiments are especially striking. Training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36% to 99% of coordinates and can reduce leverage by as much as 7x. The same setup also induces an apparent alignment between update magnitudes and the diagonal Fisher, an effect that disappears when fp32 master weights are used. This suggests that some observations about updates concentrating on important parameters may partly be numerical artifacts.

The recipe reproduction is also strong. Re-running the released OLMo-2-1B DPO recipe from the released SFT checkpoint reproduces the released delta’s displacement, leverage, and sign structure. A simpler recipe at the same anchor yields leverage that is 5x to 6x lower. Leave-one-component-out controls point to two key contributors: length-normalized loss and a batch size of 128.

Finally, leverage predicts delta reuse. For DARE-style random drop-and-rescale, the paper derives a relative damage estimate of about (1-p)/(pρsign), where p is the keep rate. Wherever DARE works, this estimate is usually within about a factor of two of the measured damage. The paper also validates the exact Fisher-form computation against finite differences: when finite differences are above the numerical floor, 649 out of 659 checks agree within 4%.102:T681,This one deserves a careful read.
